client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, it's really good to see you again. I want you to know — coming back today? That actually takes a lot. How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here, right? My mom basically made me come again but... I don't know. Fine, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you wasn't sure you'd come back, and yet here you are. Since we last talked — has anything been sitting with you? Anything you've been thinking about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Not really. I mean, everyone at school is still talking about how I got caught, which is... so embarrassing. But like, what am I supposed to do? Half the people at that party weren't even caught and they drink way more than me. It's completely unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels really unfair — like you got singled out when drinking is just... something everyone around you does.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly! Like, I'm not some alcoholic. I had three drinks. Three. And now I have to come here like I have some massive problem. It's kind of ridiculous, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three drinks and suddenly you're the one sitting here... I hear how frustrating that is. What was it like for you that night — what made you want to drink?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's just... that's what you do? Like, everyone had a cup. You don't just stand there like a loser. People would think I was weird. I just wanted to fit in, I guess. Which is — I don't know, that sounds kind of stupid when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. Wanting to belong, not wanting to feel left out — that's such a human thing. And you noticed something just now, saying it out loud... what was that like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of... weird? Like I've never actually said it that way before. It just came out. But I still think the whole situation is way blown out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted a little when you said it... I'm curious — outside of the party stuff, how are things going for you? Like, really going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...honestly? Not great. My parents have been fighting a lot. Like, a lot a lot. And school is — I used to actually like school. Now I just kind of go. The party stuff was just... it was nice to not think about everything for a little while, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So drinking gave you a break. A way to just... step outside of all that noise at home, even for a few hours. That makes a lot of sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I know that's probably not — like, I know that's not the best reason. But when you're going through stuff and everyone around you is just having fun and not caring... it's easy to go along with it. I think I've been using it to cope or whatever. Which is kind of scary to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to say. Seriously. And the fact that you can see what's been driving it — that's not nothing, that's actually a big deal. What would it look like, do you think, if things were different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... maybe actually dealing with stuff at home instead of just avoiding it? And I want to go to college next year. I don't want to be the person who messes that up. I don't want this to define me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect some of this back to you... You came back today, even when part of you didn't want to. You're carrying a lot right now — things at home, pressure from friends, wanting to fit in. And underneath all of that, there's a version of you who knows this isn't quite where you want to be. Someone who cares deeply about her future. That's a lot of important stuff.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... when you put it like that. I do care. I think I've just been pretending I don't, because it's easier? But I actually do care about my future. A lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You care more than you've been letting yourself show. So — what feels like one small thing, just one, that might look different going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... actually talking to someone when things get bad at home. Instead of just waiting for the next party. I don't know. Maybe even talking to you. That could be something.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time today. I know telehealth can feel a little weird at first, so I appreciate you just... showing up. Your advisor mentioned some concerns, but I'd rather hear it from you — what's been going on lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... honestly I'm not totally sure why I'm here. Like, my advisor made it sound like a bigger deal than it is. I've just been stressed. Work stuff, social stuff. I drink sometimes at parties, it helps me relax, but it's not like I'm showing up to work drunk or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So drinking is something that helps you take the edge off socially, and the concern feels a little overblown to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. I'm not, like, blacking out every weekend. It's more that... okay, I'll be honest, I pretty much can't go to a party or even a work happy hour without having a few drinks first. Or during. Like before I even get there I'm already having a glass of wine at home just to, I don't know, get myself out the door. Which — I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know something about that pattern feels off. That takes honesty. What does it feel like — those moments before you go out, when you're having that drink at home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terrified, honestly. Like my brain just goes through every possible way I'm going to embarrass myself. What if I say something dumb, what if nobody talks to me, what if I'm just standing there like an idiot. The alcohol kind of... quiets that? And then I can actually be a person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The alcohol gives you access to a version of yourself you actually want to be. And without it, that version feels completely out of reach.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. God, yeah. That's kind of exactly it. And that's fine, right? Lots of people have a drink to loosen up. I don't see why it's such a big deal. My friends do it too and nobody's sending them to therapy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's true that social drinking is really common. I'm not here to tell you your friends are doing something wrong. I'm curious though — you said earlier that you know how it sounds. What part of it worries you, if any?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... okay, there was this thing a few months ago. My team had this last-minute dinner, like two hours notice, and I just — I panicked. I said I was sick. I wasn't sick. I just couldn't get enough drinks in before it to feel okay about going. And I missed this whole team bonding thing and my manager mentioned it twice after. That sucked.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So when the alcohol wasn't available as a buffer, you avoided the situation entirely. And that had a real cost — professionally, and I'm guessing it didn't feel great about yourself either.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, it didn't. I felt like such a loser. Like everyone else just shows up and does the thing and I'm at home freaking out because I didn't have time to pre-game a work dinner. That's... that's not normal, is it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What you're describing sounds like the alcohol has become the only tool you have for managing really intense anxiety. That's not a character flaw — it worked, and it worked reliably. The problem is it's starting to shrink your life.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Shrink my life. Yeah. Um... I've actually been turning down a lot of stuff lately. Like my roommate invites me to things and I just say I'm tired. But I'm not tired. I'm just — I don't want to have to drink that much again, but I also can't go without it, so it's easier to just stay home. Which is also lonely. So that's great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're caught between two things that both feel bad — drinking more than you want to, or isolating. And you've been white-knuckling that alone for a while. That's exhausting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It really is. I just... I want to be able to go to dinner with my roommate without it being a whole thing. I want to show up to a happy hour and not feel like I'm going to die if I don't have three drinks first. Is that something that's actually possible? Like for someone like me?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yes. Genuinely, yes. What you're describing — the anxiety driving the drinking — that's very treatable. There are approaches, like CBT for social anxiety, that are specifically designed to build that tolerance without alcohol as the bridge. You wouldn't be doing it cold turkey and alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. I mean — that's kind of a relief to hear. I think I assumed I'd just have to, like, white-knuckle every party for the rest of my life or never go anywhere. I didn't realize there was an actual thing you could do about the anxiety part.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came in thinking this was maybe overhyped, but you've named some real things — relying on alcohol just to leave the house, missing work events, pulling back from your roommate. Underneath that is anxiety that's been running the show for a long time. And right now, you're not asking to never drink again — you're asking to have a choice. That's a really clear and honest thing to want.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. A choice. That's exactly it. I don't want to be dependent on it. I just want... options, I guess. I actually feel a little better talking about it out loud. Which is weird because I was dreading this.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. Last time we talked, you mentioned you had a work happy hour coming up this week. How did things go?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... not great, honestly. I mean, I went, which I guess is something? But I ended up drinking way more than I planned. Like I told myself, okay, two drinks, that's it. And then it was just... I don't know. Suddenly it was four and I was the last one there and I couldn't even really remember most of the conversations I had. Which is kind of the point, I guess, but also not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you showed up — which took something — and then the drinking kind of took on a life of its own, beyond what you'd intended.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And the thing is, everyone thought I was having a great time. I was laughing and talking and my manager even said I seemed really relaxed for once. Which... I mean, great, but also that's not me, that's just... that's four glasses of wine, you know? And then I wake up the next morning and my sister had texted me like eleven times because apparently I called her at midnight and said some stuff I don't fully remember. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a lot to sit with the next morning. What was going through your mind when you saw those texts from your sister?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Embarrassment. And then just... ugh, this is so stupid. Anger, like at myself. Because I keep doing this. Every single time I think, okay this time I'll be different, I'll just have one, I'll stay sober, whatever. And I can't. I literally cannot walk into a room full of people without needing something to take the edge off. I'm twenty-six years old and I have a master's degree and I can't just... talk to people. It's pathetic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being really hard on yourself right now. And I want to name something — you just described recognizing a pattern, setting an intention, and then feeling genuinely troubled when it didn't hold. That's not pathetic. That's someone who actually cares about changing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I don't know. I guess I do care. I just don't know what that gets me if I keep ending up in the same place. Like, caring about it doesn't seem to be enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're right that caring alone isn't a strategy. So I'm curious — when you picture yourself at one of these events, not drinking, what does that look like in your head? What happens?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... I walk in and immediately I don't know what to do with my hands? And everyone's already in these little groups and I'm just standing there and I can feel my face getting hot and I'm convinced everyone can tell that I'm, like, a robot pretending to be a person. It sounds so dumb when I say it out loud. But without the drink it's like... I have no buffer. There's nothing between me and how terrifying it all feels.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The alcohol has been doing a job for you — taking the edge off that physical anxiety, giving you something to hold, buying you a few seconds before you have to speak. It's been a tool, even if it's one that's started to cost you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... actually that's a really good way to put it. It does do a job. I never really thought of it that way, I always just thought of it as like, my thing that I do. But it's doing something specific, right. It's solving a specific problem. Just not in a way that actually... helps. Long term.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Exactly. And if the job is managing that physical spike of anxiety — the hot face, the not knowing where to look — what else might be able to do that job, even partially?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I've read about breathing stuff. I always kind of rolled my eyes at it, but my therapist — my old therapist — mentioned something about, like, box breathing before stressful situations. And I think there's also that thing where you just... give yourself a task? Like, if I'm handing out drinks or helping set something up I feel weirdly more okay. Because I have a reason to be moving around. Is that a thing? Does that actually work?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It absolutely is a thing. Giving yourself a role lowers the stakes of every individual interaction — you're not just standing there being evaluated, you're doing something. That's a real strategy people use.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, that's actually kind of exciting? Like, what if I just... volunteered to be the person taking food orders or whatever. Nobody thinks that's weird, it's just helpful, and then I have something to say to every person. That feels... I don't know, that feels doable. More doable than just standing there willing myself to be normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just went from describing yourself as pathetic to designing your own coping strategy in about fifteen minutes. That's worth noticing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah. I guess I did. I mean, it might not work. I might still panic and order a drink anyway. But it feels like at least I'd have a... a thing to try first. Before I just go straight to the wine. Which I haven't really had before. A before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came in today pretty shaken by last week — the overshoot on drinking, the texts from your sister, that familiar feeling of being stuck in a cycle. And by the end of this conversation you've named what the alcohol is actually doing for you, which is managing a specific, real anxiety response, and you've started sketching out an alternative — having a role, a before strategy, something to reach for first. The goal isn't perfection at the next event. The goal is having that one thing to try. Does that feel right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it does. I'm still scared, like I'm not going to pretend I'm suddenly fine. But I think I want to try it. I actually think I want to try it, which is... kind of new.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I want you to know that means something to me. Last week felt... heavy, I imagine. And you still showed up today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. My friends basically made me a group chat about it. Like, a whole intervention group chat. So. Here I am. I figured if I came back maybe they'd all just... calm down a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A group chat. That's... what's it been like, carrying that this past week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Annoying. Like, I love these people, I really do, but they don't — they don't get it. My whole brand is going out, being present, being, like, the fun one. That's not a problem, that's literally my job. I post about brunches and rooftop bars and — I don't know. It felt like they were attacking me. My whole life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The people you love looked at your life and said they were scared. And it felt like they were saying your whole self was wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean. Kind of. And the thing is — what am I supposed to do with that? Like, okay, so what if I drink at events. Everyone does. I'm not — I'm not some sad person drinking alone in the dark. I'm out, I'm social, I'm thriving. That's what it looks like from the outside and honestly? That's what it is. I don't know why everyone has decided to make it into this whole... thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You love them. You said that first — before anything else. Even when it hurts, you're holding onto that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Of course I love them. That's why it — that's why it sucks. My best friend, Maya, she was crying. Crying. And I just kept thinking, like, I'm the one who should be upset right now, not you. You're doing this to me. But she's sitting there with mascara running and I'm the bad guy somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm curious about something. When you imagine your life — who you are, what makes you you — where does drinking fit into that picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's everywhere? Like, it's not even a thing I think about. It's just — Tuesday is wine with the girls. Thursday is a brand event. Friday and Saturday are whatever. Sunday brunch. It's the rhythm of my life. It's how I connect with people. It's how I unwind. It's how I, like, show up as myself. Without it, I don't even know what a week looks like. That sounds bad when I say it out loud but it's not — it's just, that's my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's not just something you do. It's how you know who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I hate that you said it like that. Because now it sounds like — I don't know. What even is there without it? Like, genuinely. I built everything around this. My followers, my brand deals, my friendships — it all lives in that world. And if I just, what, quit? Who is that person? I don't know her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just — hold all of this for a second with you. You came back, even though it's hard. Your friends are scared and that hurts because you love them. Drinking is woven into everything — your work, your friendships, how you feel like yourself. And underneath the frustration there's this quiet question: who would I be without it? That's... that's not a small thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean. When you lay it out like that it sounds — I'm not saying you're wrong. I'm just saying it's more complicated than my friends made it seem. They acted like I just needed to stop and everything would be fine. Like it's that simple. It's not that simple.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's not simple. Not even close. Can I ask — has there been a moment, even just once, where you felt something shift? A morning, a night, something small that just... stayed with you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... There was this one Saturday. A few months ago. I woke up and I couldn't really remember the end of the night, and that's — okay, that happens, whatever. But I was in my apartment and it was like, two in the afternoon, and it was so quiet. And I just laid there. I didn't want to post anything. I didn't want to text anyone back. I just felt really, really empty. And I couldn't tell if that was the hangover or if that was just... me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were alone with yourself. And you weren't sure what you'd find there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... I hadn't thought about it like that but. Yeah. I texted my friend like an hour later to make plans because I couldn't just sit with it. I don't — I don't really do silence. But maybe that's the thing, right? Like, maybe that's — I don't know. I don't know what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You do know what you're saying. You said it. That took guts — to go there, even just for a second. You don't have to know the whole answer right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not — I'm not saying I have a problem. I want to be clear about that. But maybe... maybe I could figure out why that morning felt the way it did. Like, just that. Just that one thing.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi there, I'm so glad you came in today. I'm Margaret — I work here at the clinic. There's really no pressure at all, no agenda. I just want to get a sense of who you are and what's been going on for you, at whatever pace feels comfortable. Can you start by telling me a little about yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Yeah. I'm Barbara. I'm fifty-five. I... I don't really do this kind of thing, talking to someone like this. I saw something online about the clinic and I almost didn't come. I almost turned around in the parking lot, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you didn't turn around. What was it that finally made you walk through that door today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My sister. She said something last week that kind of... I don't know, got under my skin. She said I smell like wine when she calls me in the evenings. Which — I mean, a lot of people have a glass of wine at night. It's not... it's nothing. But it bothered me that she said it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about what she said stuck with you. Enough to bring you here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. She worries too much, she always has. But... yeah. Okay, maybe I've been having a little more than just a glass. I don't know. It's a way to wind down. There's nothing wrong with unwinding.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The evenings sound like a particularly hard time. What's been going on this past year that's made them so difficult?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My... my husband died. Eight months ago. Frank. He just — it was a Tuesday morning, he was having his coffee, and... heart attack. He was sixty-one. We had things planned. And I come home to an empty house every single day and I just... [trails off]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You come home, and he's not there. And the wine... it helps quiet that, at least for a little while.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. It really does help, for a little while. I'm not — I'm not some kind of alcoholic or whatever. It's just... without it I lie there and think about him and I can't turn my brain off. I can't sleep. So. It's just practical.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was Frank like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh god. He was... he was so funny. The dumbest jokes. [laughs softly, then quiets] He used to leave little notes on the coffee maker before I woke up. Just stupid little things. 'Have a good one, Barb.' And I used to roll my eyes. And now I would give anything to find one of those notes. Anything. [long pause] I haven't really talked about him much. Nobody wants to hear it anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nobody wants to hear it anymore. You've been carrying all of that... alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. My kids are dealing with their own grief, and I don't want to be a burden, so I just... I stopped calling as much. And they got busy. And I pulled away from everyone, really. The wine is easier than trying to explain how I feel. But I don't think it's actually helping. I just wake up the next day and he's still gone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty to say — that maybe it isn't actually helping. And I want you to know, what you just shared about Frank, about those notes... I'm honored you told me that. You don't have to carry that by yourself in here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think part of me knows. I didn't used to drink like this. Frank would have hated it, honestly — he was healthy, he ran 5Ks. And I look in the mirror sometimes and I just... I don't recognize myself. That's a strange thing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's not strange at all. If things were a little different — if you felt a little more like yourself — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd... probably call my daughter more. She keeps inviting me to things and I keep saying no. And maybe I'd go back to my book club — I stopped in January. I just didn't feel like being around people. But I miss it. I miss having somewhere to be. I miss having a reason to get dressed in the morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I've heard today, Barbara. You've been through an enormous loss — Frank, your partner, your person — and the grief has been almost unbearable to carry on your own. The drinking started as a way to get through the nights, and a part of you is beginning to see that it may be keeping you more stuck than it is helping. You've pulled back from your kids, your book club, the people who love you. And underneath all of that, I hear someone who misses herself. Who misses having reasons to show up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet] Yeah, that's... that's about right. I didn't think I'd say all of this. I came in thinking I'd just get checked off some list. But... I think I want to try. I don't know what that looks like yet. But I think I'm ready to at least talk to someone. Really talk.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you making time for this today, especially... I know this probably isn't where you imagined yourself being. What brought you here — in your own words, not what anyone else has told you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My therapist basically told me I had to come. Which, fine, whatever. I got a DUI three weeks ago and everyone's acting like I'm some kind of... I don't know, like I'm Lindsay Lohan or something. It was one night. I had two glasses of wine at a work thing and I got pulled over. That's it. That's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two glasses of wine, a work event, and now suddenly you're being treated like your entire life is a problem. That feels really unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Thank you. Like, I work incredibly hard. I have a real job, I pay my rent, I'm not — I'm not some drunk. My friends drink way more than me, honestly. Nobody's making them come to therapy. It just feels like because something bad happened, now I'm the poster child for alcoholism or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned your friends — tell me a little more about what drinking looks like in your world. What does a typical week look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's marketing. That's just — that's the industry. We have client dinners, happy hours, like it's literally part of the job. And then yeah, sometimes after a brutal day I'll have a glass of wine at home to decompress. Is that a crime? God, I feel like everything I say in here is just going to be used against me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
...

You're worried that being honest here means being judged. That whatever you say, someone's already decided who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Haven't they? My parents won't stop calling. My boss knows — which is humiliating, by the way — and my roommate keeps leaving pamphlets on the counter like I'm not going to notice. Nobody's asked me how I'm actually doing. They're just... waiting for me to admit something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds exhausting. Carrying all of that — the embarrassment, the feeling of being watched, everyone waiting — and still showing up here today. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I guess. I didn't really have a choice, but... I don't know. It has been a lot. The night it happened I was just — I genuinely thought I was okay to drive. And then the lights came on and I just... I can't really describe what that felt like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that like — those few seconds when you saw the lights?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terror. Pure terror. And then this weird... shame. Like, before they even said anything, I knew. I knew it wasn't just two glasses. I'd had more at the pre-event thing and I just kind of... I don't know, I stopped counting at some point. I've never admitted that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You knew. Even in that moment, part of you knew. And you've been carrying that — the real version of that night — while everyone around you only has the version you could bear to tell them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm so tired of it. The keeping track of what I told who. My mom thinks it was literally one drink. And part of me knows that's — I mean, that's not right. But I just couldn't. I couldn't say it. Because then it becomes a different conversation and I'm not ready for that conversation.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — and stop me if I'm getting this wrong — there's the story you've been telling, which protects you from the harder conversation. And then there's something underneath that you're starting to wonder about. Not because anyone forced you to, but because you've been living with it for three weeks and it's getting heavy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. That's... that's pretty accurate. I think about that night a lot. Like, not the DUI part, but the part where I poured the third drink and thought 'I should slow down' and then just... didn't. That happens more than I want it to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you notice that — that moment where you think 'I should slow down' and something else takes over — what's usually going on for you right before that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Stress, mostly. Or like... social stuff. I get really anxious in big work events, which is ironic because that's half my job. And the drink kind of... it turns the volume down on that. The problem is it turns the volume down on everything, I guess. My judgment included. I never really connected those two things before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just did something really significant. You drew a line — not because I drew it, not because your parents or your roommate drew it — but because you looked at your own experience honestly and you saw something real. That's not nothing. That's actually where everything starts.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know what to do with that yet. But... I don't know. Maybe that's okay for today. I'm not saying I have a problem. I'm just saying maybe I've been using it wrong. Or too much. I need to think about it.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this is your first session since finishing detox, and I imagine that's not a small thing. How are you doing right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't really know why I'm here. My brother basically dragged me in. I mean... I did the detox, I did what they asked. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because your brother wanted you to be, and part of you is wondering what the point is — you already went through detox.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I mean, I wasn't like... I'm not an alcoholic or whatever. I just... things got out of hand for a while. The divorce, everything. Anyone would've done the same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The divorce hit you hard. What happened — if you're willing to talk about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She just... up and left. Twenty-two years. Two kids. And she just decided she was done. Took the house, took the kids most of the time. I'm in some apartment now that smells like someone else's cooking. It's — I don't know. It is what it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. Your whole adult life, basically. And now you're in a place that doesn't feel like yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — yeah. It doesn't. I keep forgetting where I put things because nothing's in the right place, you know? Stupid thing to notice but.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not stupid at all. What's it been like, day to day, living through all of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Hard. Really hard. I'd come home from work and there was just... nothing. Silence. And I'd think, okay I'll just have a drink to take the edge off, and then... I don't know. One became six became I wake up on the couch at 3am not knowing what day it is. I didn't plan for it to get like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't plan for any of this. And you still got yourself through detox — that takes real guts, especially when everything else is falling apart.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean — my daughter called me. She said she was scared. She's sixteen. She shouldn't have to be scared of her own dad, that's not... that's not right. That's the thing that got through, I think. Not anything else. Just her voice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your daughter's voice. What does that tell you — about what matters to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I'm failing them. Both of them — I've got a son too, he's nineteen. He doesn't really call anymore. I think he's angry at me. And I get it, I do, but it still... it still hurts like hell. I lost my wife and I'm losing my kids too and I don't know how to — I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The anger's been covering something. Under all of it — the drinking, the blame — there's a man who's grieving. Grieving his marriage, grieving the distance with his son, scared of losing his daughter too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [long pause] ...Yeah. Yeah, I think that's right. I've been so — I've spent four months being pissed off at her. And underneath that I'm just... I'm devastated. I don't even know who I am right now without all of it. The house, the family, the... the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in today not sure why you were here. But you've told me you're living somewhere that doesn't feel like home, that you've lost connection with your son, that your daughter's fear woke something up in you. You're not just someone who drank too much — you're someone in the middle of a profound loss, trying to figure out who you are now. And you still showed up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... I mean, I knew things were bad, but I kept telling myself it was her fault, it was just the situation. I don't know. Maybe I need to actually deal with this. Like really deal with it — not just white-knuckle it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Really dealing with it — what would that look like for you? What would be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Being present, I guess. Not numbing out every night. Maybe... calling my son. That terrifies me honestly. But — I want to be someone my kids aren't scared of. I want to be a dad again. I don't know if that's even possible at this point, but... I want it.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back today. Last week took some courage, and here you are again. Before we get into anything, I just want to check in — how are you doing since we last spoke?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... okay, I guess. I don't know. I've been kind of in my head about everything. Like I almost didn't come today, honestly. I just kept thinking, what's the point, you know? But then I was sitting in my studio and I couldn't paint anything and I was like... fine. Fine, I'll go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something in that moment — sitting in the studio, nothing coming — pushed you to show up anyway. That's worth noticing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah. It's been like that a lot lately. I sit down with a glass of wine, which is... that's always been my thing, that's how I get into the zone. And I just stare. The canvas just stares back. I've done three paintings in the last two months and I hated all of them. I painted over two of them. That never used to happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built your whole creative process around drinking — it's been part of your identity as an artist for a long time. And now that process is... not working the way it used to. What's that like to sit with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's terrifying. Because if the drinking isn't helping me make art, then what is it doing? And then I think — no, wait, it IS helping, I just need to find the right... the right headspace again. I've had slumps before. Every artist has slumps. This isn't — I'm not saying it's the alcohol's fault.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding two things at once — the fear that the alcohol might not be helping anymore, and also the need to protect a belief that's been central to how you work. That's a really uncomfortable place to be. I want to share something with you, if that's okay — some of what we actually know about alcohol and creativity. Would that be alright?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Sure. Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the idea that alcohol unlocks creativity is genuinely widespread — it's a cultural myth that goes back centuries. Hemingway, Pollock, the whole arc of it. And in the short term, early on, alcohol does lower inhibition, which can feel like freedom. But what the research actually shows is that over time, and especially with daily use, alcohol starts to suppress the prefrontal cortex — the part of the brain responsible for complex thought, nuance, the ability to self-evaluate your work. The very things that make a painter know when something is good.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So you're saying... the reason I can't tell if my work is good anymore — that could be the drinking? Not just like, a slump?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's a real possibility worth considering. You said yourself — you painted over two canvases. You've never done that before. What do you make of that, in light of what I just shared?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I thought I was just losing my touch. Like some fundamental thing about me had broken. But if it's — if there's an explanation that isn't 'you're not talented anymore'... God. That's both better and worse somehow. Because then it's on me to actually do something about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real honesty to say. And I hear something in there — you're not someone who wants to stay stuck. The fact that you came back here, that you're connecting these dots right now — that tells me a lot about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I've been an artist my whole life. Since I was eight years old. It's not what I do, it's who I am. And the thought of changing how I work, like fundamentally changing it — what if I try painting sober and it's just nothing? What if the work is flat and empty and I hate it even more?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the fear isn't really about the alcohol — it's about your identity. What if the art doesn't survive without it? That's the real question underneath all of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. ... But then I think about the ER. Waking up there. That was — I've never been that scared. And I looked at my hands and I thought, these hands are supposed to be making things, not... this. So I don't know. Maybe the art I'm protecting isn't even real anymore. Maybe I've been protecting a memory of what it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing across everything you've said today, because I think it matters. You came in not sure why you were here. You talked about the studio, the blank canvas, the paintings you destroyed. You told me you're terrified of losing your art. And then just now, you said maybe you've been protecting a memory, not the real thing — and you thought about your hands, what they're meant to do. That's an enormous amount of insight in one session.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it all together like that... I sound like someone who already knows what she needs to do. I just don't know if I'm brave enough to do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Bravery isn't the absence of fear — you showed up here afraid, twice. What would one small step look like for you this week? Not a big declaration, just... one thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... one morning. Just try one morning in the studio without opening a bottle first. See what happens. I'm not promising anything big, but — one morning. I can do one morning.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for coming in. I know you said you were squeezed for time, so... I just want you to know we can go at whatever pace feels right. There's no agenda here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I have like forty minutes before my next thing, so. I'm here. I don't totally know why, honestly. My husband basically made this appointment for me, which is... I don't know. It feels a little patronizing? Like, I'm a grown adult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like this wasn't really your idea. What's your sense of why he wanted you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The DUI. Obviously. Which, look — that was one night. One night out of, I don't know, twenty-eight years of being a completely functioning person. I made a bad call, I'm dealing with the legal stuff, I'm paying the fines. I don't understand why that means I have to come talk to someone like I'm... broken or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One mistake out of twenty-eight years. And now everyone's treating you like something's fundamentally wrong with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And I get it, like — I know it was bad. I'm not an idiot. But Marcus keeps acting like I'm some kind of... alcoholic, and it's like, no? I drink at work events, I drink with friends, that's what people in their twenties do. That's what marketing people do. It's literally part of the job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up anyway. Even feeling like this was someone else's call, not yours. That's... actually something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I mean. Yeah. I didn't really have a choice, but — I guess. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned Marcus. What did he actually say to you? Like, the conversation that made you think — okay, I'll go.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He said he couldn't do this anymore. Those exact words. 'I can't do this anymore.' And I was like, what are you even talking about, it's one DUI — but he brought up... other stuff. Times I came home and didn't remember things, or whatever. And I just — I don't know, I think he's being dramatic. We've been together six years. You don't just leave over stuff like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six years. And hearing him say 'I can't do this anymore'... that must have landed really differently than anything he's said before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. It did. Because he's not — Marcus doesn't say stuff like that. He's not dramatic. He's the most un-dramatic person I know, which is why I married him, so when he said it I kind of... I don't know. Part of me went cold. Like, oh. Oh, he means it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you went cold like that... what were you most scared of losing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Him. Obviously. I mean... him. And also — god, this sounds so stupid — but like, the version of myself that has it together? I have a good job, I work really hard, I'm good at what I do. And somewhere in the last couple years it's like... I don't know when drinking went from being fun to being the thing I need at the end of every day. I didn't really notice it happening.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't notice it happening. It crept in slowly, and now you're standing here wondering how you got here — this person who has everything figured out professionally, but something shifted. And you're not sure when.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's kind of exactly it. I keep telling people it was one mistake but I think what I'm actually scared of is that it wasn't. That it's been a lot of smaller mistakes for a while and the DUI just made it impossible to ignore. And I hate that. I really hate that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real honesty to say that out loud. Especially for someone who's used to having things under control. What would it mean for you — not for Marcus, not for the legal case — but for you — to actually look at this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think it would mean admitting that I'm not as okay as I tell everyone I am. Which is terrifying. But also... I'm so tired. I'm tired of the hangovers and the anxiety the next morning and wondering what I said at the last work happy hour. I don't want to be forty and still doing this. I actually don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in here defensive — and honestly, that made sense, this wasn't your choice. But somewhere in this conversation you named something important: that part of you already knows the DUI wasn't random, that something's been building, and that you're exhausted by it. You're not ready to call it anything yet, and you don't have to. But there's a part of you that showed up today not just for Marcus — but maybe for that version of yourself you don't want to lose.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I think that's right. I don't know what I'm going to do, but — can I come back? Like, next week? I think I want to keep talking about this.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know you just finished the detox program, and I imagine walking through that door took some courage — especially with everything you've got going on right now. I want to be upfront: there's no agenda here, no judgment. This is your space. So... what's on your mind as you sit down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... honestly? I don't really know why I'm here. I mean, I know why — my coach basically said I had to, and then the whole thing with my labs freaked everybody out — but like, I feel fine. I felt fine before all of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there were a couple of things pushing you here — your coach, and those lab results. What was it like getting that news from the doctor?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it was weird. They made it sound like way bigger of a deal than it probably was. Liver enzymes elevated or whatever. But I'm twenty years old, I work out every single day — I think my body can handle some stress. My teammates drink way more than I do, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're comparing yourself to your teammates, and part of you feels like your body should be able to bounce back — you're young, you're built for this. And still, something about those numbers was unsettling enough that it stuck.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah, okay, fine, it was scary. But that doesn't mean I have a problem. Everyone goes through phases, right? College is stressful, the season is stressful. I'm not some... I'm not an alcoholic or whatever people are trying to make me out to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The label 'alcoholic' feels like it doesn't fit, and I'm not here to put one on you. I'm more curious about something you mentioned — the team, the season. How has all of this been affecting your performance, from your own perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's the thing that actually gets to me. Like I don't care about labels or whatever, but... my forty time has gone up. My reaction time is off. Coach pulled me from the starting lineup two weeks ago. That has never happened. Not once, my entire career.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being pulled from the starting lineup when that role is such a core part of who you are — that must have hit hard. And the fact that you can see that connection, and that you still care this much about your game... that says something real about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, it did. I cried in my car after practice. Which is — I haven't done that since like middle school or something. I don't know. It just felt like... who even am I if I'm not performing out there?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Who am I if I'm not performing — that's a really profound thing to be sitting with. I'd like to explore that with you. What does being an athlete actually mean to you, beyond the stats and the starting lineup?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... everything, honestly. Like, football is the thing I worked for my whole life. My dad drove me to six AM practices when I was eight years old. I got a scholarship because of this. I have guys on my team who are like brothers to me. And I feel like I've been... slowly letting all of it just slip through my fingers. And I'm the one doing it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real — years of sacrifice, a scholarship, relationships that run deep. And underneath all the noise about labs and coaches, what you're actually describing is watching yourself drift away from something that's core to who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it, actually. Like, the going out felt like part of the team thing, you know? Blowing off steam after a game. But at some point it stopped being about that, and I don't really know when. That's kind of... that's messed up that I can't even pinpoint it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I've heard from you today, and you tell me if I get it wrong. You came in feeling like this was largely forced — the coach, the lab results, everyone else's alarm bells. And underneath that, there's a part of you that knows something has shifted. Your performance is slipping, you cried in your car. Football is everything you've worked toward — it's your brothers, it's your dad at six AM, it's who you are. And somewhere along the way, what started as blowing off steam started costing you the very thing that matters most. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That tracks. I'm not gonna sit here and pretend I have it all figured out. But yeah. That's where I'm at. I don't wanna lose this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want to lose this. And you just did something that's harder than it looks — you sat with some really uncomfortable truths without running from them. So given everything you've just said, what feels like one thing you'd actually be willing to think about or try differently, starting this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think I need to just... be real with my guys. On the team. Because half the time I go out it's 'cause I don't want them to think I'm bailing. But if I actually told them what was at stake — like, really told them — I think they'd have my back. I think they want me to succeed. That feels like somewhere to start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Trusting that the people you care about will show up for you if you let them in — that takes real courage. You walked in here today not even sure why you came, and you're leaving with something concrete that you actually want to do. That didn't come from me. That came from you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I still got a lot to figure out. But I feel like — I don't know, for the first time in a while I actually feel like I might be able to do this. Like there's a path or something.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for jumping on. I know doing this from home is a little different — some people find it easier, some feel like they're in a fishbowl. So, what made today the day you decided to reach out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm not sure I needed to. My wife — partner, she prefers partner — she found some article online and basically sent me the link with a look. You know the look. So here I am. But I want to be upfront, I'm not here because I think I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. And honestly, showing up at all — even because of 'the look' — that takes something. A lot of people get that link and close the tab.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah, well. I've built a company from eight people to three hundred. If I had a problem that was affecting my life, I'd know. My quarterly numbers are up, my team is performing, I closed a Series C in January. Whatever she's worried about, it's not — it's not showing up where it matters.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a serious track record. I'm curious — when you wind down after a day like that, what does that actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, it's... I have a drink. Or a few. Scotch, mostly. I've got a good bottle I keep in the study. It's not — I'm not sloppy about it. It's ritualistic, almost. I've earned it. I work fourteen-hour days sometimes and I need to decompress. Doesn't everybody?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A ritual you've earned. Something that helps you shift gears after carrying all of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes. That's exactly it. I don't — look, I'm not sitting in a bar. I'm at home. I'm not driving anywhere. I know what an alcoholic looks like and it's not... it's not a bottle of Glenfarclas in a home office after a fourteen-hour day. That's just being an adult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does she see that worries her, do you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She thinks it's every night. Which — okay, it is most nights, but that's... that's not the point. She says I'm different after. More distant. Less present. But honestly? I'm tired. I'm running a company. I don't have a lot of — I'm not going to be doing cartwheels at ten PM. That's not a drinking problem, that's being forty-five and exhausted.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're clearly not someone who ignores things — you run toward problems, not away from them. So it's interesting that the one thing she keeps flagging is the thing you've already assessed and cleared.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because I have assessed it. I'm not stupid about this. I know the risks, I know what dependence looks like clinically — I've had HR situations, I've had to let people go for it. I know what I'm doing. She doesn't see the full picture. She sees me tired with a glass in my hand and she catastrophizes. That's her anxiety, not my problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When she says you've become more distant — what do you think she actually means by that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She, um... she said last month — she said she feels like she's living with a roommate. That I check out. And I don't know, maybe... maybe there's something to that. After the second or third drink I just want quiet. I don't want to hear about school stuff or whatever renovation she's planning. I just want to sit. And I know that's probably not great. But I don't know how else to get through the night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't know how else to get through the night. That's... that's a different thing than 'everything's fine.'

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess it is. I haven't said that out loud before. I don't know what that means. I don't know if I want to know what it means. The days are fine — I'm great during the day, I'm sharp, I'm on. But somewhere around six or seven PM something just... the volume goes up. On everything. And the only thing that turns it down is—

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you if that changed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... Sarah would stop looking at me like she's trying to figure out if I'm still in there. I've got two kids — twelve and nine — and I want them to remember me as someone who was actually there. Not just in the house. Present. I don't know. That probably sounds cheesy coming from a guy who just spent ten minutes telling you he's fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound cheesy at all. It sounds like someone who's been sitting with this a lot longer than he let on today. You came in saying you didn't have a problem — and somewhere in the last forty minutes you've told me the nights are hard to get through, that scotch is how you manage the volume, that your partner feels like she's lost you, and that you want your kids to remember you as present. That's not nothing. That's actually quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I didn't... I didn't expect it to go like this. I thought you'd give me a pamphlet and I'd feel good about having shown up. I'm not ready to say I have a problem. But maybe I've been managing something. And maybe the way I've been managing it isn't — isn't the only way. I don't know. Maybe we talk again.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I just want to say — that matters. A lot of people don't. How are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine. I don't know. My lawyer said it might look good if I'm, like, actively seeing someone so. Here I am. Not that I think I need to be here, I just — it's complicated.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's complicated. I'd love to understand what complicated looks like for you right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's just — everyone's acting like I'm some kind of... alcoholic or something. My mom keeps calling. My boss pulled me aside. And it was one night. One. I've driven after drinks a hundred times and nothing ever happened. This time I just got unlucky.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Everyone's looking at you differently now. And underneath all of that... there's something that feels really unfair about it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like, I work hard. I've built my career from nothing basically. I don't — I'm not some person who, like, sits at home and drinks alone. I go out. I network. That's literally part of my job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking has been woven into so much of what you do professionally. I'm curious — when you think about last week, and how things have changed... what's been the hardest part to sit with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? The embarrassment. Like, I had to call my dad to pick me up from the station at midnight. He didn't say anything. He just... drove. And that was somehow worse than if he'd yelled at me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That silence from your dad... sitting in that car with him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't — can we not talk about my dad? That's not — this isn't about him. I'm fine, I just made a mistake. People make mistakes. I'm not going to sit here and like, unpack my childhood or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: We don't have to go anywhere you don't want to go. I just noticed something shift when you mentioned him. We can stay right here. ... What do you want me to understand about that night that you feel like no one's getting?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I was having a terrible week. Like, really terrible. We lost a huge account at work and I'd been killing myself on it for months, and everyone just... moved on. And I needed to decompress. I needed to just turn my brain off for a few hours and I — I misjudged. Okay? I misjudged.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You needed relief. Real relief. And drinking — when it works — what does it actually give you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... turns the volume down. On everything. I stop replaying stuff. I stop thinking about what I should have said, what I should have done differently, whether people think I'm good enough. It's like... an hour where I'm just not so loud to myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty to say. That voice in your head — the one that questions whether you're good enough — that sounds exhausting to carry around every day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It kind of is. I don't really talk about that part. People at work just see the confident version. I've gotten really good at that. But yeah. It's... it's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to bring together what I'm hearing. You came in today partly because of the legal stuff, but you also came back — and I think that means something. You're someone who works incredibly hard, who carries a lot of pressure, and you've found that drinking turns down a voice that never really goes quiet. And last week, that caught up with you in a really public, really scary way. And you're still processing what that means — not just legally, but about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... I don't know. I guess I've been so focused on defending myself that I haven't really let myself think about whether — like, whether this is actually a pattern. I don't want it to be a pattern.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want it to be a pattern. ... If it were — even a little — what would you want to do about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know yet. But I think... I think I'd want to figure out how to make that voice quieter without it. Because I can't keep — I don't want to be someone who needs it. I don't want to be that person.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this probably wasn't your idea... and I just want you to know, you don't have to pretend anything in here. We can just... be honest with each other. So — what's it like, being here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It sucks. I don't want to be here. My parents made me come and I think it's stupid. I've done this before and it doesn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through this before... and it didn't help. That's... that's a really exhausting place to be. Showing up somewhere you don't believe in, again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Last guy just kept asking me how I felt about my feelings or whatever. Like, dude. Come on. And my parents act like I'm some kind of... addict or something. I had some beers. It's not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're sitting — your parents are blowing this way out of proportion. And the last counselor felt... kind of useless. Like he was going through motions.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Pretty much. I mean... I don't know. Whatever. They found the bottles and now suddenly I'm like, a problem. But every kid drinks. My friends all drink. Nobody's sending them to therapy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels unfair. Like you got caught and now you're the one sitting in this chair, when other kids are doing the same thing and nobody's saying a word to them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Kind of. I mean, yeah. It is unfair. But also like... I don't know. Whatever, forget it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You started to say something and then pulled back. I'm not going to push you... but I noticed. And I'm not going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... I hide the bottles in my room, right? Like, I'm not drinking at parties or whatever. I'm mostly just... doing it alone. In my room at night. Which is — I know how that sounds. It's fine, it's just a habit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Alone. At night. ... That image — a kid by himself in his room with a bottle — that lands heavy for me. What's it like... in those moments, before you crack one open?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. It's like... quiet? And not the good kind. Like the house is quiet but there's still all this... stuff. Like my parents fighting downstairs, or just the way everything feels kind of... heavy. And then after a couple drinks it's like the volume goes down. Everything goes down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The volume goes down. ... That's such an honest way to put it. It sounds like drinking gives you some relief from something that feels really loud inside.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I guess. I mean yeah. I don't — it's not like I'm depressed or whatever people want to say. I just... I don't like how things feel sometimes. And it helps. That's all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you — you're not putting a label on it. And I'm not going to either. But I want to ask you something, and you can totally tell me it's none of my business... How long have things felt that heavy?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... A while. Like... I don't know. Since my parents started — um. Yeah. A while. Maybe like a year? More maybe. I kind of stopped counting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A year of carrying that... and finding your own way to get through the nights. That actually takes a kind of strength, even if it's costing you something too. And I wonder — part of you, the part that almost said something earlier and then pulled back — does any part of you wonder if there's another way?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Sometimes. Like sometimes I wake up and I feel kind of sick and I'm like... this is dumb. I'm sixteen. This is — I don't want to be like, doing this when I'm thirty, you know? That would be really sad. I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can already see that future — and it scares you. That's not nothing. That's you, at sixteen, having enough self-awareness to say: this isn't who I want to be. I think that matters a lot. And I think you knew something was off before your parents ever found those bottles.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I did. I just — I didn't want to admit it. To them. To anyone. It's embarrassing. Like what kind of person hides bottles in their room and drinks alone at sixteen. That's... that's kind of messed up, right?

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. I know this might feel a little... unexpected. Maybe not exactly what you signed up for. There's no agenda here, nothing you have to say or prove. Can you tell me a little bit about what brought you in — in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My sister basically dragged me here, so. I don't know. She's worried about me, I guess. I kept telling her I'm fine. I'm handling things. But she wouldn't drop it, so... here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She cares about you enough to push. And you love her enough to actually show up, even if you'd rather not be here. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I showed up. Doesn't mean there's some huge problem, though. I work full time. I take care of my kids — two kids, by myself. I come home and I have a glass of wine to unwind. That's just... that's normal. People do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. Working full time, raising two kids alone, holding everything together... and then coming home to quiet down after all of that. That's a lot to carry. Every single day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. That's just life, right? It's not like I have a choice. Their dad's not in the picture. My family's not close by. It's just me. And I don't... I don't really see how that changes. Like, I don't see a version where this gets easier. This is just what it is now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
... 

That loneliness sounds really heavy. Like you've been running on empty for a long time and nobody's been asking how you're doing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't even let myself think about it most days. I just... I get through. Get them fed, get them to bed, and then I just — I need something that's mine. Something that makes everything stop for a minute. Is that so bad?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment when they're finally asleep and you can just... breathe. You deserve that. You really do. I'm wondering — what would it mean to you if you could have that quiet, that relief, and still feel okay in the morning?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if that's possible, honestly. I've tried just like... watching TV or whatever, and my brain won't shut off. I'm running through everything I didn't do, everything that's coming tomorrow. The wine just... it turns the volume down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your mind is so full. You've been the one managing everything for so long that even stillness feels kind of... unsafe. Like if you stop moving, it all falls apart.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And I know — okay, I know a bottle a night is too much. I'm not naive. I see myself in the morning and I'm just exhausted and I feel like garbage and I think about my kids and I just... I don't want them to look back and remember their mom like this. I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — your kids looking back at you — that came from somewhere real. What kind of mom do you want them to remember?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: A present one. One who was actually there. Not just... physically in the room going through the motions. I want to actually be there. Like, remember things. Be awake for it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Present. That's such a meaningful word. And the fact that you can name that so clearly — you can feel the difference between going through the motions and actually being there — that tells me you haven't lost sight of what matters most to you. Not even a little bit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I care so much it's like... it physically hurts sometimes. Which is kind of the whole problem, right? Everything just feels like too much and I don't have anywhere to put it so I just... I pour a glass and it goes away for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying all of that feeling with nowhere to put it. So if we could find another way — something that actually holds it instead of just quieting it for a night — what do you think that might look like? What feels even a little bit possible for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe talking to someone. Like really talking, not just pretending I'm fine. My sister's been telling me to do therapy for like two years. I always said no because I thought it meant I was broken or something but... I don't know. Maybe I was just scared.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today not even sure you belonged here — maybe a little frustrated at your sister for pushing you. And now you're sitting here telling me you want to be present for your kids, that you've been holding this alone for a long time, and that maybe you don't have to. That took something. I want you to know I don't take that lightly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... I didn't expect to feel like this when I walked in here. I still don't think I'm like — I'm not some alcoholic or whatever. But maybe... maybe I need to figure out a different way. For them. For me too, I guess.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, make yourself comfortable — I promise the couch is better than it looks, despite what it's been through. I'm glad you made it. First time doing something like this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Um... I almost didn't, honestly. My daughter's friend is the one who — she's a therapist herself, and she thought I should come talk to someone. I don't really know what I'm supposed to say. I'm not even sure I belong here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's no script, which is either very freeing or mildly terrifying depending on the day. You don't have to have it figured out. Can you just tell me a little about what's been going on for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... I have a lot of pain. My back and my hip, for years now. I take what the doctor gives me but sometimes it — it doesn't quite touch it, you know? So I have a glass of wine in the evening. Sometimes two. To take the edge off. I didn't think that was... I mean, it's wine. It's not like I'm doing anything terrible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the medication alone isn't cutting it, and you've found that the wine fills in that gap. When you're dealing with pain that just doesn't let up, that makes a certain kind of sense.

utterances.speaker: client
