utterances.text: Exactly. I'm not — I raised three children. I kept a house. I wasn't some person who just... this wasn't planned, any of it. And now my daughter called me last week, crying, saying she was frightened. And I felt awful. I still do. But what does she want me to do, just sit there and hurt?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That phone call really landed on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Of course it did. She's my youngest. I spent my whole life making sure I was never a burden to anyone, and now — now at 72 I'm the one everyone's worried about. It's humiliating, if I'm being honest. I never wanted to be the problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've spent decades making sure everyone else was okay. And now the people you love are scared for you — and somehow that feels like you've failed, even though you're the one who's been quietly suffering.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yes. That's — yes. I keep thinking if I were stronger, or if I'd figured out a different way to manage... I probably should have said something sooner. I just didn't want to make it about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying this very quietly for a long time. What made you decide to actually come in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Her voice on the phone. She was so scared. And I thought... if something happened to me, she'd never forgive herself. Even if it wasn't her fault. And I don't want to do that to her. I really don't. So here I am. Even if I have no idea what I'm doing here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The love you have for her — wanting to protect her from that kind of grief — that's not a small thing. That's actually a really strong place to be standing right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's a good girl. They all are. I just... I don't know what I'm supposed to do differently. The pain isn't going to disappear. I still have to wake up with it every morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're right — the pain is real, and we're not going to pretend otherwise. So let me ask you this: if things started to shift — not magically, not all at once — but if you got to a place where you felt more on top of this... what would that actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd like to not feel like I'm hiding something. I'm so tired of being sneaky about it. And... I'd like Sunday dinners where nobody's watching me the whole time. Where I'm just grandma again. That sounds silly when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound silly at all. You want your life back. Not a perfect life — just yours. Where you're not hiding, not being monitored, not managing everybody else's worry on top of your own pain.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. That's — I didn't expect to say it like that but yes, that's it exactly. Is that... is that something that's actually possible? At my age, with all of this?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me tell you what I heard today, because I want you to really take this in. You came in unsure if you even belonged here. And in one hour you named what's driving the drinking, you named what it's costing you, and you told me exactly what you want. That is a lot of work. And to answer your question — yes. There's genuinely a lot we can do, including looking at the pain management side of things so the wine doesn't have to carry that whole load. You don't have to keep doing this alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Okay. Okay. I'm not making any grand promises, but... yes. I think I'd like to try.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for coming in. I know the counselor over at the VSO office referred you, and I just want you to know — there's no agenda today. We can go at whatever pace feels right. What brings you in, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I came because they said I had to. That's — that's the only reason I'm sitting here. Gerald passed eight months ago and now everyone's got an opinion about how I'm living my life. I don't see what talking is going to do about any of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't choose to be here, and part of you is wondering what the point of any of this is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. I'm not — I'm not some kind of... I like a glass of wine in the evening. Maybe two. My husband just died. That's not a problem, that's — that's a normal person dealing with something terrible. But all of a sudden everyone's sending me to clinics.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like the people around you are concerned, and that's landing as — as judgment, maybe. Like they're saying something's wrong with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It IS judgment. My son calls me every week going on about how I'm not returning messages, I'm 'not myself.' Well — no. No, I'm not myself. My other half is gone. Thirty-two years. What does he want me to be? I'm supposed to just bounce back? Gerald was sick for a long time before the end and I was there for every single — I did everything right. And now I'm the problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were there for all of it. Every hard day of his illness, every single one. And now you're being asked to justify how you're getting through your own grief.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. That's — yes. Thank you. Because nobody seems to understand that. They want me to go back to being who I was before Gerald died and that woman doesn't exist anymore. She's just... gone. So yes, I have a drink at night. I don't see why that's anyone's business but mine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking isn't really what we need to talk about right now — you've been carrying something enormous, alone, for a long time. I'm just curious... what does a night actually look like for you these days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I... the house is quiet. It's always quiet now. I'll watch TV for a while and then I can't sleep because — everything just comes back. His last few months were bad. Really bad. And at night my brain just... replays things. Things I saw. Things I couldn't fix. So I have a drink and it... it turns the volume down a little. That's all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The wine isn't really about the wine. It's about finding some quiet from the memories. From those last months.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, I guess that's... I've never put it like that. I keep telling myself it's just a habit, just something to do. But um... I know I'm drinking more than I was. A year ago I barely touched the stuff. I know that. I'm not stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not stupid at all. You know yourself. And it sounds like part of you has been watching this shift happen, even while another part has needed it to keep happening.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter came by last month. I'd cleaned up but I missed — there was a bottle I didn't get to. She didn't say anything. But she had... she has her father's eyes, you know, same exact eyes. And she just looked at me and I... I fell apart. I didn't want her to see that. I don't want to be a burden to my kids. They've already lost their father.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to share. You're protecting everyone around you — your kids, your grief, Gerald's memory. And underneath all of that, you're a woman who has been watching herself change and doesn't quite know how to stop it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want my daughter to remember me like this. I don't want — I worked hard my whole life. I was a good wife, I was a good mother and I just... I feel like I've disappeared since he died. Like there's nothing holding the edges together anymore. And the drinking... okay. Okay, it's not helping. I know that. I do know that. I just don't know what else to do with the nights.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you could imagine something different for those nights — not fixing everything, just something a little different — what would that even look like to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to stop being so afraid of the quiet. That's — I think that's the real thing. It's not the grief exactly, it's the silence where Gerald used to be. I just want to be able to sit in that room and not feel like I'm... drowning in it. Does that make sense? Maybe if I could do that I wouldn't need the... I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes all the sense in the world. The silence is where he used to be. You're not fighting the drinking — you're trying to survive the absence. And today, for the first time, you're sitting with someone and saying that out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I haven't talked about him. Not really. Everyone wants to check on me but nobody wants to actually talk about Gerald. Like he just — like we're all pretending there wasn't a whole person there. And I've been so angry. I'm still angry. But I'm tired too. I'm really, really tired. Drinking alone in the dark... that's not how I want to be. That's not who I want to be.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you again, Maya. You mentioned when you texted that this past week was... rough. I want to make sure we have space for that today. Can you tell me a little bit about what's been going on for you since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I... um. So the thing at work, the incident they reported me for, that's — my supervisor actually sent a formal email to HR about it. So now there's like, a record. And I've been trying to just keep working, keep painting, but honestly I'm kind of terrified that this is going to follow me. I don't know. I just feel like everything is kind of... teetering.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's real fear there — that this is now on record, that it could define how people see you professionally. And underneath all of that, you're still trying to show up and create. That sounds like a lot to carry at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. And like — I know what they think happened. They think I came in impaired, which is... I mean, okay, I'd had a couple glasses the night before, but that's just... that's how I unwind. That's how I get my head right for the next day's work. I've always done that. It's not — I'm not some, like, stumbling around person. I function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you — functioning, showing up, maintaining your routine. I want to come back to that in a moment because I think it matters. But you also mentioned in your message that the painting itself has been... not going well. What's been happening there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's the part that's... that's what's really getting to me, honestly. I looked at a canvas I finished last month and I didn't recognize it as mine. Like, it was technically done. But it felt... hollow? Muddy. I used to have this precision, this like, intentionality in every stroke. And now it's just... I don't know. Something's off and I can't figure out what.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real courage to say out loud — that something you love, something that defines you, doesn't feel like yours anymore. You noticed that. A lot of people wouldn't let themselves see it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been telling myself for years that drinking is part of the process. Like, it loosens something. Lowers the filter so I can get to the real stuff underneath all the... the overthinking. But lately I'm wondering if... I don't know. If I've been lying to myself about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really significant thing you just said. You've held this belief for a long time — that alcohol is what unlocks your creativity. I'm curious: where did that idea come from for you? Like, how did it become part of how you understood yourself as an artist?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... okay, so in my early twenties, like MFA school, everyone drank. It was kind of romanticized, you know? The tortured artist thing. And I did some of my best work then. So I just... I connected those two things. I assumed one caused the other. But now that I'm actually thinking about it — I was also twenty-three. I had all this energy and hunger and time. Maybe... maybe that was the real thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So for over a decade, the drinking and the creativity got fused together in your mind — they happened at the same time, so you believed one was producing the other. And now you're starting to pull those apart and ask: what if that equation was never actually true?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And that's... kind of a devastating thing to realize. Because if it was never the alcohol, then what have I been doing? I've been using it as this — like a permission slip, almost. Like it gave me license to go deep. And maybe I just could've... gone there myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you think back to a piece of work that you're genuinely proud of — something that felt true and precise and like you — what do you remember about the conditions when you made it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was this series I did, god, maybe eight years ago. I was going through a breakup. I remember being... clear. Like, painfully clear. I wasn't numbing anything, I was just feeling all of it and putting it directly on the canvas. And those paintings — people still ask me about those. They're the ones that meant something. And I wasn't... I wasn't drinking heavily then. I actually think I barely drank that whole stretch.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just connected something really important — that the work people respond to most came from a place of being fully present, not filtered. That clarity you described? That was you. That's been inside you this whole time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I don't know why I'm surprised to hear that, but I kind of am. I think I'd forgotten. Or I stopped trusting it. Like somewhere along the way I decided I needed a crutch, and then the crutch just became... the whole thing. But those paintings were real. I made those. That was me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard today, because I think you've done something really significant in this room. You came in carrying real fear about the work situation, and then you did something hard — you looked honestly at the relationship between your drinking and your art. You named that the belief may have been a story you told yourself, not a fact. And you remembered a version of yourself who created powerfully without that. That's a lot of ground to cover, and you moved through it with real openness.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I've been scared that if I stop, the art stops. Like, what if I get sober and I'm just... ordinary? But right now, in this moment, I'm more scared that if I keep going, I'll lose the art anyway. And I'd rather try and find out than just... watch it disappear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real shift — moving from fear of losing something by changing, to recognizing the cost of not changing. Given everything you've said today, what feels like one concrete step you'd actually be willing to take before we meet again next week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to try one day. Just — one day without it. And I want to go to the studio that day. Not to produce something great, just to... see what it feels like to be there sober. To see if anything comes. I think I need to know if she's still in there.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. I know the ER is... not exactly how anyone wants to spend a night. How are you feeling right now, physically, emotionally — whatever comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I feel fine. I mean, I'm fine now. This is... I don't even know why I'm here, honestly. My roommate basically dragged me and the nurse said I had to talk to someone before they'd discharge me or whatever. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here because it felt like you didn't have much of a choice. That makes sense. And I want you to know — you're not in trouble here. This isn't like... a disciplinary thing. I'm just curious about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well, everyone's acting like I almost died or something. I had too much to drink at a party, that's it. It happens. Like half my floor has ended up in worse situations than me and nobody's making them sit in a... therapy office.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels unfair. Like you're being singled out for something that's just... normal around you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because it is normal. I'm a senior, it's spring semester, everyone drinks on weekends. That's literally just college. My friends did this whole... intervention thing last month and I was like, guys, are you serious right now? You're all doing the same thing I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your friends cared enough to say something, and your roommate stayed with you last night at the ER... it sounds like the people around you are worried. What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. I think they're overreacting. Marcus is kind of like that, he's always the responsible one in the group, he doesn't even drink that much. So. I appreciate that he came but it's not like — I'm not some alcoholic. I go to class, I have a 3.2 GPA, I'm graduating in six weeks.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're handling your responsibilities, you're almost at the finish line of something really significant. That genuinely matters. And at the same time... you ended up in the ER. I'm wondering what that night was like for you — not the medical part, but like, before. What was going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was just a party. I don't... I mean, I had a lot. More than usual maybe. There was a lot going on that week, I had two finals back to back and this group project that was a complete disaster and I just wanted to like, not think about it for one night. I don't know. I wasn't trying to end up there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You needed a break from a really overwhelming week. And drinking was the way you gave yourself that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess. It's just — when I drink I don't have to think about any of it. The thesis, my parents asking about jobs every five seconds, what happens after graduation. It all just kind of... goes quiet for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That quiet sounds like it means a lot to you. Like drinking gives you the only real rest you get from all of that noise.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... when you say it like that it sounds kind of bad. But yeah. I don't know, I haven't really thought about it that way. I just — everyone's got their thing, right? Some people go to the gym, some people play video games. Mine's just... going out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like hearing yourself say that — that this is how you cope with everything that's weighing on you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Kind of... weird, I guess. Like I never really put it together before. I just thought I liked drinking. But this year specifically it's been — I've been going out more. Like a lot more than freshman or sophomore year. I don't know if that means anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You noticed something there — that it's escalated. That took some honesty to say out loud. I want to reflect back what I'm hearing from you today: you came in not wanting to be here, you've been carrying a lot — the pressure of finishing school, your future, your family's expectations — and drinking has been the thing that's helped you manage all of that. And last weekend, something happened that put you in the ER. I don't want to put words in your mouth about what any of that means. But I'm curious what you think... about all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I don't know. I'm not ready to say I have like a problem or whatever. I still don't think it's that serious. But I guess... maybe the way I've been doing it lately isn't — I don't know. I don't know what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to have it figured out. That's okay. You came in here today, you stayed, and you said something real just now — even if you're not sure what to do with it yet. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I don't know. Maybe. I'm still not — like I'm not promising anything. But I guess I can come back. Maybe. We'll see.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this wasn't your choice. Before we get into anything specific, I'd like to hear it from you — what's your understanding of why you're sitting here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My understanding? Some judge decided two DUIs means I gotta spend my Thursdays talking to a shrink instead of, I don't know, living my life. That's my understanding. I don't have a problem. I had two bad nights.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because the court said so, not because you think you need to be. And that feels deeply unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It is unfair. I did two tours in Iraq. I came home, I got a job, I pay my taxes. The second one — I was barely over. Point-oh-eight. You know how many guys I knew who drove way worse than that every weekend? Nobody's dragging them in here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to be clear — I'm not here to convince you of anything or tell you what to decide. That's not how I work. But I am curious about something, and it's not about the legal stuff. Since the second DUI, what's actually been going on for you? Day to day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My wife and I are not — things are tense. She hasn't said it's about the DUI but it is. And I had to tell my supervisor at work, which was... that was a great conversation. Real highlight of my year. Other than that, fine. Everything's fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's been real fallout. At home, at work. Things shifted after that second incident.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I'm not some drunk, okay? I work every day. My kids are taken care of. I coach my son's flag football. One mistake and now I'm — I don't know, I'm supposed to be this cautionary tale? The system doesn't care about any of that. It just sees a number on a breathalyzer.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been holding a lot together — showing up for your kids, your job, doing it largely on your own. That takes real effort. Especially carrying whatever came back from the service on top of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Nobody — you just do it. Nobody gives you a medal for functioning, right? You just get up and you handle it. And then at the end of the day you need to decompress somehow. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say decompress — what does that actually look like for you on a regular evening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'll have a few beers, watch the game. Whatever. I'm not hiding bottles, I'm not drinking at work. My dad did it, his dad did it. That's just — that's how guys like us wind down. It's normal. It's not like I'm, you know, falling down or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a pattern that goes way back — using alcohol to come down after carrying a hard day. And at the same time, I'm noticing you brought up your wife, your job, your supervisor... like part of you is tracking whether this is costing you something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife says I'm different after the third or fourth one. More... I don't know, she says I get distant. Check out. I don't feel like I do but... I mean, I can't exactly watch myself from the outside, so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You've worked hard to hold things together — the job, the family, coaching your son. You're proud of that, and rightly so. And at the same time, there are cracks showing up: your wife is pulling away, your supervisor knows, and now you're questioning whether you can really see yourself clearly when it comes to the drinking. That's a lot to be sitting with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. When you put it all in a row like that. I didn't — I wasn't trying to blow anything up. I was just trying to get through the day. That's all I was doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If nothing changes — if things stay exactly as they are right now — what does that look like five years from now? For you, your marriage, your kids.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I don't want to think about that. I grew up with a dad who checked out. Sat in his chair, had his drinks, just — wasn't really there even when he was there. I swore I'd be different. I am different. But I don't... I can't let my kids look at me the way I looked at him. I won't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here furious at a system you didn't choose, and even so, your kids are right there in the room with you. You're thinking about who you want to be for them. That's not nothing. That's actually the most important thing you've said today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I just don't want to lose everything before I figure it out. Maybe — I don't know. Maybe there's something worth talking about here after all.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really good to meet you. I'm glad you came in today. I just want you to know there's no pressure here — we can go at whatever pace feels right for you. I'm curious... what was it like, making the decision to come and talk to someone?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly? I didn't really decide. My friend Priya, she kind of... she made the appointment. I just — I showed up, I guess. I don't really know if I need to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Priya cared enough to make that call, and you cared enough to walk through the door. Those are two separate things, and I don't want to skip past that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. She's — she's the only real friend I have here, so. I didn't want her to think I was just ignoring her. She got really scared. But like, I don't think what happened was as bad as she made it out to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you two have a real connection, even from a distance. Can I ask — what's it been like living here, building a life in a new place, mostly on your own?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... I don't know. Hard? I came here thinking it would get easier after a few months but it didn't. I go to work, I come home, and it's just... quiet. Like, a specific kind of quiet that gets into you, you know? And I don't — back home I had my family, my cousins, everything. Here I have my apartment and Netflix.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That specific kind of quiet... it sounds suffocating. Like the silence has weight to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly that. And I think — okay, I know the drinking got out of hand. I know. But when I'd have a few glasses, that quiet would just... go away for a while. And I could actually breathe. I wasn't planning for it to turn into... all of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found something that worked, for a little while, when nothing else was. And you're also sitting here telling me it went somewhere you didn't want it to go. That takes honesty — real honesty — to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't said that to anyone. Not even Priya. She just saw the... the outside of it. She didn't know the why. I don't think I even knew the why until just now, saying it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really significant thing you just put into words. I'm sitting with that. ... When you imagine your life here — not the way it's been, but the way you'd actually want it to feel — what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to feel like I belong somewhere. That's it, really. I want to wake up and not feel like a visitor in my own life. I want — god, I want to have people. Like actual people who would notice if I didn't show up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Belonging. Being seen. People who would notice. ... That's not a small thing to want. That's a very human thing to need.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I kept telling myself I was fine being independent. Like, I moved across the world by myself, I can handle anything, right? But I think I was just — lonely. Really lonely. And I didn't let myself call it that because it felt like failing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You made an incredibly brave move coming here alone. And underneath that strength, there was this loneliness you were carrying in silence, because naming it felt like weakness. The drinking was a way to soften that — not a character flaw, but a coping strategy that eventually cost more than it gave. And now, after detox, after Priya, after today — there's a part of you that's starting to ask what it might look like to actually build the life you came here for. Does that feel close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's it. I didn't think anyone would — I don't know, I didn't think it would make sense to someone else. But hearing you say it back like that, it doesn't sound crazy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense. ... I'm wondering — as you think about moving forward from here, what feels like one small thing that might help with that loneliness in a way the drinking never really could?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There's this — okay this sounds stupid — there's an Indian cultural group that meets near my apartment. I walked past the flyer like ten times and kept telling myself I was too tired. Maybe I could actually go. And I guess... keep coming here. If that's okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound stupid at all. That sounds like someone who knows exactly what she needs and is finally letting herself reach for it. I would very much like to keep meeting with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. ... Okay. I think I can do that.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you again, Dorothy. Your daughter mentioned things have been a little harder this past week. I'd like to hear from you directly — how have things been going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... I don't want her worrying about me, that's the thing. She's got her own life, her own kids. I've just been... it's been a harder week, yes. The pain in my hip has been something awful, and I — I may have had a little more to drink than I should have. I know that's why she called you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot — the physical pain, and on top of that, worrying about being a burden to your daughter. That matters to you, not wanting to put that on her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. It really does. She's got enough on her plate. I just... when the pain gets bad at night, I don't know what else to do. I take my pills, but they only do so much, and a couple glasses of wine takes the edge off enough that I can sleep. I'm not — I'm not drinking all day or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've found something that helps you get through the nights, and sleep feels essential when you're dealing with that level of pain. I want to be honest with you about something, though — you mentioned mixing the wine with your pain medication. That combination is something I do need to ask you more about, because it can be genuinely dangerous. Is it okay if we go there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yes, alright. I suppose I knew you'd bring that up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you know about what that combination does to the body — at your age, with the medications you're on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... well, I know it's not ideal. The pharmacist said something once. But I figured a glass or two isn't the same as — I mean, I'm not a young person doing something stupid. I've been managing my health for 72 years. I know my own body. But... I'll be honest, this past week scared me a little. I woke up and I didn't remember getting to bed. That hasn't happened before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took courage to say out loud. Waking up and not remembering — that frightened you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Yes it did. I lay there and I thought — what if something had happened? What if I'd fallen? Nobody was home. And then I thought about my daughter finding me and... I can't do that to her. I just can't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So even in that moment of fear, what came to the surface was her. Protecting her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She lost her father six years ago. I am all she has left. And I keep telling myself I'm fine, but... maybe I've been telling myself that because it's easier than asking for help. I've never been good at asking for help.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to recognize about yourself. You've gotten through a lot by being self-sufficient — and somewhere along the way, asking for help started to feel like the wrong thing to do. What would it mean, for you, if you did ask for help with this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think it would mean admitting that I can't do everything on my own anymore. And that's hard. That's very hard at my age. You spend your whole life being capable and then one day you realize you've been white-knuckling it for years and nobody knew.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard you say today. You came in because your daughter was worried — but you've told me you were already scared yourself after that night you don't remember. You've named that the drinking is connected to pain, to sleeplessness, and to not wanting to burden anyone. And you've said that protecting your daughter is the thing that matters most to you. That all fits together in a way that's really clear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... it sounds like I've been making things worse while trying to make them manageable. I don't know. Maybe I have been.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'd like to talk with you about some options for the pain management piece — working with your doctor to find something that actually helps you sleep without the risk. Would you be open to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think I would. I don't want to have another night like that. And... I think I'm ready to let my daughter help a little more. I've been pushing her away and calling it protecting her, but maybe that's not quite right either.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That right there — that shift in how you're seeing it — that's not nothing, Dorothy. That's exactly the kind of thing that's hard to arrive at, and you did it today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm there yet. But I'm... I'm tired of being so afraid all the time and pretending I'm not. That's a start, isn't it?

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for getting on with me today, Marcus. I know... doing this over a screen isn't quite the same as being in a room together, but I want you to know I'm fully here with you. There's no rush. How are you feeling, just right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine, I guess. A little weird. I've done this before — therapy, I mean — so it's not like I don't know what to expect. It's just, my sister kind of pushed me into this one, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your sister was worried enough to make that call for you. What's it like, being here because someone else reached out on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Kind of annoying. I don't — I mean, I get it, she cares. But I'm a grown man. Thirty-nine years old. I've been handling my stuff for a long time without anyone stepping in. It's not like I'm... I don't know. It's complicated.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. Complicated. That word feels right for a lot of things, I imagine. You've been through therapy before and it didn't hold — and yet here you are again anyway. Something in you kept that door from closing all the way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... I don't know if I'd say it was something in me. More like I got tired of arguing about it. But the last therapist — it just felt like she was checking boxes. 'Rate your mood one to ten.' And I'd just lie, because, what's the point. I don't really trust that this is gonna be different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You learned to protect yourself in those rooms. Keep it on the surface, get through it. I don't blame you for that. And still — you didn't fully close the door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. Look — the drinking thing, it's not... it's not what everyone's making it out to be. When I'm really low, and I mean really in the dark, like the depression stuff is bad, a few drinks is the only thing that actually turns the volume down. I know how that sounds. I know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not here to take that away from you or tell you it's bad. I'm genuinely curious — what does it feel like when the volume goes down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... relief. Like actual relief. Like I can breathe for a little while. And I know — I'm not an idiot — I know that's probably a problem. But when you're in it, you're not thinking about tomorrow. You're just trying to get through tonight.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Getting through tonight. Just that. ... There's a real exhaustion underneath what you're describing — trying to survive your own mind, night after night. That's an incredibly heavy thing to carry alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, it is. And the thing is, nobody — they don't see that part. My sister sees me drinking and she sees a problem. She doesn't see what's happening before that. What's been happening for like fifteen years. The depression. I've been really alone with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fifteen years of carrying something that heavy, mostly in silence. And you're still here. You still showed up today. I don't want to move past that too quickly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... some days barely. There have been times where I... yeah. But I'm still here. I don't always know exactly why. But I think about my kids. What it would do to them. That's usually what pulls me back when it gets really bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just hold everything you've shared for a moment. You've been living with depression for fifteen years, mostly alone with it. Drinking has been the thing that gives you relief when nothing else does. Therapy hasn't felt safe — you learned to protect yourself in it. But you have kids, and they anchor you. And you're here today, not because everything's okay, but maybe because something is starting to shift.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. Yeah, that's — that's actually accurate. I'm tired. I'm really, really tired of it being like this. I don't want my kids to grow up watching me disappear into myself. I've already done enough of that to them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like if things were even a little different? Not fixed — I'm not talking about fixing everything. Just... a little different than tonight.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'd want to wake up and not feel like I'm already behind before the day even starts. Like, just one morning where I felt okay. I haven't had that in so long I don't even remember what it feels like. But I want that. I actually want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing — wanting something, even something that still feels far away. That's exactly where we start. I'm really glad you stayed in this conversation today, Marcus. I mean that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Me too, actually. Which is... I didn't expect to say that. So. I don't know — maybe this is different. Maybe I'm different enough now that it can be. We'll see, I guess.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. You'd mentioned last time you were going to have a tough week — how did it go?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Not great. I mean, it wasn't, uh — yeah. Not great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about what happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just — there was a lot going on. End of quarter grades, a parent complaint, my department head was on my case about something... I ended up drinking more than I planned to. Which, I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were under a lot of pressure, and the drinking went further than you intended.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, it's not like I blacked out or anything. It was just a few extra glasses. I still made it to work. I function fine. I just — I don't know, maybe I leaned on it a little more than usual this week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even when things pile up, you keep showing up. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... I don't have a choice, do I? I've got 120 kids who need to be somewhere and someone has to be in that room. I'm not going to just fall apart. [pause] But I did come in Thursday feeling pretty rough. Like, rough enough that one of my eighth graders asked if I was okay. A thirteen-year-old. That... that kind of stayed with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that like — having a student notice?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Embarrassing. Honestly, kind of... I don't know. Scary? I've been teaching for eleven years. I'm good at this. I care about these kids. And the idea that one of them is looking at me thinking, like, 'what's wrong with Mr. H' — that's not, that's not who I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one hand, this week felt like a slide — more drinking, more stress, coming in rough. And on the other hand, that moment with your student landed somewhere real. Something about who you are as a teacher, what you stand for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. I've always been the teacher that kids trust, you know? I had a teacher like that when I was their age and it made a difference. I don't want to be the guy who's just going through the motions.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you — your life, your teaching — if the drinking wasn't something you had to manage around?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Huh. I haven't thought about it like that. I think I'd just be... less tired? Like, I wake up most mornings feeling like I already owe the day something. If I wasn't doing that every night I might actually... I don't know, have some energy. Feel like myself again, maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Feel like yourself again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — I don't even know when I stopped, you know? It just kind of... crept up. Started as a glass of wine after work, that was fine. Then two, then whatever was in the house. And I kept telling myself it was just stress, it's temporary, once things calm down at school I'll dial it back. But things don't really calm down. And I keep moving the goalposts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been watching yourself do this — tracking the pattern, noticing the goalpost moving. That kind of self-honesty takes something. What feels like one small thing you might be willing to try before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not keeping wine in the house? Like, if I actually have to go somewhere to get it, I might not bother. I know it sounds almost too simple but I think that's kind of the point — make it harder for myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today after a hard week, and instead of shutting down you talked through it — the student who noticed, the feeling of losing yourself somewhere along the way, the goalposts that keep moving. And now you're naming one concrete thing you can actually do. That's not nothing. That's movement.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, it is, isn't it. [small laugh] I don't know if it'll work but — I think I want to try. I'm tired of being tired, you know?

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — I literally watched you speed-walk past the window. I'm Maya. And I want to say upfront, if you glance at the clock more than three times in the next forty-five minutes, I won't take it personally.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah — parking was a nightmare and I have Intro to Psych right after this which is kind of ironic, I guess. I'm Sarah. And honestly I don't really know why I'm here, like, I know why I'm here, but... ugh.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Intro to Psych right after this — that is genuinely funny. Okay, Sarah. Court referral. That's kind of the world's most awkward way to end up in a therapist's office. What's your version of what happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it was one incident. I had a 0.09, which is barely over the limit, and I think the whole thing got blown way out of proportion. Like, I wasn't weaving or anything. I just — my sister called and I thought I was fine to drive over and I wasn't. But one mistake doesn't mean I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're standing, the consequence feels like a lot compared to what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Kind of. I mean, I own that I shouldn't have driven. I'm not — I'm not trying to say I did nothing wrong. But the context matters, right? I have a four-month-old at home. I'd been up since like 3am. It was a rough night and I just needed a break.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about that night. The one before it happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She wouldn't stop crying. Like, three hours of solid screaming — they think it's colic — and my husband was in Chicago for work and I just... I poured a glass of wine. And then another one. And I kept thinking, once she goes down I'll feel better, but she wouldn't go down, and then my sister texted and I thought the fresh air would help and I just... I made a really bad call.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Completely alone, no backup, running on fumes — and you were still trying to find a way through it. That's an exhausting place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It is. She's... she's actually really great, like, I love her so much it's insane. But nobody tells you how hard it is. The wine just — it's like, I can breathe for a second. Turn my brain off. I know that's probably not what you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you being straight with me. What does a typical evening look like for you now — like, walk me through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Feed her, try to get her down, she wakes up, I pour a glass. Sometimes two. It's every night now. And I know how that sounds, I do — I'm not stupid. I'm a functional person. But... every night wasn't really the plan. That kind of snuck up on me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about hearing yourself say 'every night' — it lands differently than you expected.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, like... she's four months old right now. She doesn't know anything. But she's not always going to be four months old. And I don't want her to grow up and — I don't know. My mom wasn't a big drinker or anything but I still noticed when she was stressed, you know? Kids notice. I don't want to be the mom she has to notice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull this together for a second. You've had a genuinely brutal four months — no sleep, solo nights, real postpartum stress, and one night that ended with a decision you regret. The wine has been doing a job for you, taking the edge off when nothing else is available. But when you look forward, at who you want to be for your daughter as she gets older — that's where it stops feeling okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's — yeah. It's kind of bleak when you lay it out like that. But also weirdly accurate. I hadn't really let myself think about it that far forward, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if you did decide to do something differently — what would that even look like for you? Not what the court wants, not what your husband wants. What does it look like for Sarah?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'd actually want to sleep. Like, actually sleep. And I want to feel like myself again, not just like survival mode on a loop. And I want her to see me as someone who has her shit together. Sorry — language.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here rushed, sleep-deprived, technically required to be here — and in twenty minutes you went straight to your daughter and who you want to be for her. That's not a person without direction, Sarah. That's someone who knows exactly what matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Huh. I don't know, I never thought about it like that. Maybe — yeah. Maybe I actually want to figure this out. Not just because of the court stuff. Because of her.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab a seat anywhere, make yourself comfortable. I'm Marcus Torres, most people just call me Marcus. So your PCP sent you over... what's on your mind today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, yeah. So Dr. Patel ran some bloodwork and she said my liver enzymes were a little elevated and she wanted me to... talk to someone. I don't really know what that means for me exactly. I'm a bartender so, you know. Kind of comes with the territory, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Comes with the territory. So there's something about the job that makes it feel kind of... expected?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah? Like everyone I work with drinks. It's just — after a long shift you need to decompress, right? But I don't know. Something made me actually look at it recently and I was like... huh. I couldn't remember the last day I didn't drink. And that just kind of... sat with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that like — when that thought hit you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Weird. Kind of... I don't know. Unsettling? Like I wasn't expecting to feel that way about it. I've always been the guy who's like 'I can stop whenever' — and I mean I still think I could — but the thing is I just... haven't. Not once. Not in like... I don't even know how long.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took some real honesty to sit with. A lot of people would've just let that thought go.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I mean it's not like I'm drinking at 8am or anything — I'm not... I don't think I'm an alcoholic. But my girlfriend said something a few weeks ago, kind of offhand, and it stuck. And then the bloodwork thing happened and I was just like, okay. Maybe I should actually talk to someone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sounds like a few different things have been stacking up. What worries you most out of all of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? The not-remembering part. Like... I'm 27. I feel like I should be able to name a Tuesday where I just didn't. And I can't. That feels like it means something, I just don't know what.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Like there's a line somewhere you might have crossed without really noticing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And the thing is I love my job, I'm good at it. But I'm starting to wonder if I've just kind of... built my whole life around having a drink available. Like it doesn't even feel like a craving — it's more like it's just what I do. And I'm not sure when that happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things stayed exactly the same a year from now — same job, same pattern — how do you see that sitting with you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Not great. I think that's actually why I'm here. Like... I've watched people come through my bar for years and you can kind of tell who's there because they want to be and who's there because they don't know where else to go. And I'm starting to wonder which one I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if I'm hearing you right — a few things have been stacking up: the bloodwork, something your girlfriend said, and this moment of realizing you couldn't name a sober day. And underneath all that is this bigger question — is this actually who I am, or is this just something I've drifted into? And part of you isn't sure you like the answer.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's pretty much it. I haven't really said all that out loud before. Kind of hits different when you hear it back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — even just a small version of it — if things were a little different for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think just... having a choice about it. Like I want it to be a decision, not just a default. Even if I still have a beer after work, I want it to be because I actually want one — not because I don't know how to end a shift without one. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes a lot of sense. And honestly — that distinction you just made, between choosing and defaulting? That's not a small thing. That's actually a really clear picture of what you want. You walked in here not knowing what to expect, and you've already put your finger on exactly what matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I have. I didn't think I'd feel better after this but... I don't know. Maybe I should've said this stuff out loud a long time ago. So what do we do from here?

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let's start where you are today. How have things been going since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly, it's been kind of a mixed week. Like, there were a few days where I actually did okay — I stuck to the plan — but then toward the end it kind of... fell apart. I don't know. I feel like I keep taking one step forward and then, I don't know, something just... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there were some real wins in there — days where you actually followed through — and then something shifted toward the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. The first few days I was feeling pretty good about it. Like, I managed to not open anything until after Mia was down for the night, and honestly I didn't even want it as much? But then my mother-in-law came to stay and everything just kind of went sideways.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about those first few days — what do you think made them different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I just had more of a routine going. I was busy, Mia was sleeping a little better, my partner was home in the evenings. I wasn't sitting there alone in the kitchen at nine o'clock feeling like I was gonna crawl out of my skin.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's actually really significant — you figured out what conditions helped you. The routine, the connection, not being isolated in those late evening hours. That took real self-awareness.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess so. But then I kind of threw all of that out the window, so — [exhales] Sorry. I'm just frustrated with myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What happened when she arrived?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She just... she has this way of making me feel like I'm doing everything wrong. She'd come in and pick up Mia and I could see her looking around at the kitchen, the dishes, and I'd feel this — this tightness in my chest. And the first night I just had two glasses and then a third and I... yeah. It snowballed from there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The feeling of being watched, judged — it was overwhelming. And the wine felt like the only thing in that moment that could take the edge off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. And I knew it was happening — like I could literally hear this voice saying 'you don't need this' — but I was so tired and I just wanted five minutes where I wasn't thinking about whether I was doing everything right. And then I'd feel worse in the morning. Mia would be up at six and I'd have this headache and just... this horrible guilt. Looking at her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you're sitting there with her in the morning — what is it you want for the two of you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... God. [long pause] I want to be present. Like, actually present, not just going through the motions. She's starting to do this real smile now — not just gas, like a real smile — and I want to be the kind of mom who's fully there for that. Not someone who's half-asleep and ashamed of herself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You've identified what helps — routine, connection, not being alone late at night. You know what makes it harder — stress, feeling scrutinized, isolation. And underneath all of it is this very clear picture of who you want to be for Mia. That's not a small thing. That's actually a lot to work with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... I don't know, it doesn't feel hopeless, I guess. I think I've been treating this week like proof that I can't do it. But maybe it's more like... I know what went wrong. Which is different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Exactly. You're not starting from zero — you're starting from experience. That's different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think I need to have some kind of plan for when it feels like that — when she's there, or when that tightness shows up. Because if I don't have something to do instead I just... I default to the wine and then it spirals and I lose all the ground I made.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So thinking about the next time a moment like that comes up — what feels like it could actually work for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I could text my sister. She's been really supportive and sometimes just saying it out loud to someone helps. Or even just go to another room, put something on, give myself like thirty minutes before I make any decisions. I think I just need to slow the moment down a little. Like, create some space in there.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. Take a seat wherever you're comfortable. So — what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't really know why I'm here. My buddy kind of pushed me into it. Said I should talk to someone. I don't... I'm not like, a therapy person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your buddy saw something that had him worried. What do you think he was seeing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, he's being dramatic. I work at a bar. I drink after work. That's — that's just the job, you know? Every single person I work with does the same thing. You're on your feet for eight hours, you smell like booze the whole shift, customers are a nightmare — you clock out, you decompress. That's it. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's completely built into the culture — everybody does it, it's how you come down after a shift. And still, something got you through that door today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. He doesn't work in a bar. He doesn't get it. And I'm not here because I think I have some big problem, I just — I figured, whatever, I'll go once, get him off my back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. But you said you don't know why you're here — I'm curious what actually pushed you out the door this morning. Because you could've just said no.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. I... a few days ago I woke up and I was still drunk. Like, went to sleep drunk, woke up drunk. And I'm just lying there and I thought — when's the last time I wasn't? Like, an actual sober day. And I couldn't... I couldn't think of one. I sat there for a while and I couldn't find a single day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That stopped you cold. You went looking for one day and came up empty.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And that — that pissed me off, honestly. Like, I'm twenty-seven. I'm not some... I don't think of myself as a drunk. That's not who I am. But I couldn't answer my own question. I couldn't give myself an answer.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You asked yourself an honest question and you didn't like what came back. That's not nothing — a lot of people don't ask.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It doesn't feel like some big brave thing. It just felt like... like I'd been running on autopilot and suddenly noticed. You know what I mean? Like — when did this become my whole thing? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When do you think the shift happened — from 'I'm unwinding after work' to something that started feeling different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably... a year ago? Maybe a year and a half? I used to have days off where I'd just chill out, eat food, watch whatever, not drink. And then at some point I started having 'just a couple' on days off too. And then it wasn't even a decision anymore, it was just — it was just what I did. Like the default setting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The off switch just... stopped being an option you reached for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly that. Exactly. And I — I never actually said that out loud before. To anybody.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm tracking this right. You've got a job that's basically marinated in alcohol — it's the whole environment. Drinking after shifts started as a way to decompress, made total sense. But somewhere in the last year or two, the days off went the same way. No more off switch. You woke up still drunk, asked yourself a simple question, couldn't answer it, and that rattled you enough to actually show up here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if you're thinking about what comes next — not what your buddy wants, not what anyone else thinks — what would you actually want it to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I'm not saying I want to never drink again, I work in a bar, that's... I just want it to be a choice. Like, I want to be the one deciding, not just — not just doing it because that's what happens. Does that make sense?

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Reyes — grab a seat wherever feels comfortable. So, uh, the VA sent over some basic info, but I'd rather hear it from you. What brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know. My... my buddy Marcus, he had a heart attack last month. Forty-one years old. And I'm sitting there at the hospital thinking, like — I'm not that far behind him, you know? The drinking, the not sleeping, all of it. I figured maybe it's time to actually talk to someone instead of just telling myself I'll figure it out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a pretty serious wake-up call. Watching someone your age go through that — it has a way of making things feel real in a way that's hard to ignore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. I mean, look, I've been here before — not this office, but therapy, whatever. It didn't really... I did a few sessions years back and the guy just kept asking me about my mom, and I was like, that's not — I'm not here for that. So I stopped going. I'm a little skeptical, I'll be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. And honestly? I appreciate you saying that straight up rather than just sitting there nodding politely for six sessions. That takes some guts. For what it's worth, I'm not going to ask you about your mom — unless your mom is the one buying the drinks, in which case we might need to have a different conversation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. No, she's not. She's, uh... she passed a few years ago actually. But — okay, yeah, that's funny. I can work with that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm sorry about your mom. And hey, you're still here, in this chair, which tells me something about you. When you say you've been drinking — what does that actually look like for you day to day? Not the clinical version, just... what's a regular week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it starts usually after dinner. Maybe a beer or two watching TV, but then it's — I don't know, it kind of creeps up. Some nights it's half a bottle of whiskey before I realize it. It's not like I'm drinking at work or anything, I'm not that guy. It's mostly nights. When it gets quiet and my head gets loud, I guess. That probably sounds worse than it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When it gets quiet and your head gets loud — that's actually a really precise way to describe it. What's going on in your head on those nights?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... just everything piling up. Deployment stuff, some of it. But also just like — feeling like I'm behind, like everyone else figured out how to do life and I'm still sitting there in the dark. The depression, they diagnosed me with that, like two years ago. I take the pills but they don't really... I don't feel different. And then I drink and at least I feel a little less like I'm crawling out of my skin.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the alcohol is doing something real for you — it's giving you relief from something that's genuinely painful. I want to make sure I understand that, because it's not just a bad habit, it's actually solving a problem. At least in the short term.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — no one's ever said it like that. Most people just say, well you shouldn't drink so much. Like I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know the risks, you've known them for a while. And you came in anyway. That's not nothing. What would it mean for you — like in your actual life — if things were different? If the nights weren't something you had to survive?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I have a daughter. She's eight. Her mom and I aren't together but I get her on weekends and I just... I want to actually be present, you know? Not hungover. Not half-checked out. I want her to remember her dad as like — a real person. Not just someone who was there but wasn't really there. That's what I keep coming back to when I think about why I'm even doing this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being a real presence for her — that matters to you more than almost anything else you've said today. I can hear it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. I mean — yeah. It really does. I don't want to be my dad. He was there, physically, but... you know. I swore I wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, just to make sure I've got it right. You came in today because watching Marcus scared you into taking this seriously. You've tried therapy before and it didn't fit — you needed something that actually met you where you are, not some formula. The drinking isn't random, it's how you cope when the depression gets loud at night and there's nothing else in the toolkit. And underneath all of it, the thing pulling you forward is your daughter — wanting to show up for her the way your own dad didn't. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... that's pretty much it. When you put it all together like that it's kind of a lot, actually. I don't know, I feel like — I feel like maybe there's something here. Like maybe this time could be different. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That maybe is enough to start with. A lot of people walk in here with less than a maybe. So — given everything you just laid out, what feels like the right first step? Not the big overhaul, just... what's one thing that feels doable?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... actually showing up next week. I've got a habit of bailing when it gets uncomfortable. So maybe just — coming back. That's probably where I start.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, you actually came back. I half expected you not to, honestly, given how last week went. What's going on for you today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... I mean, it's not like I had a ton of choice after the whole ER thing, right? Everyone's acting like I'm some kind of... I don't know. I'm fine. I'm literally fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The ER thing clearly shook some people around you. And I'm noticing it shook you a little too, even if 'fine' is the word you're landing on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... okay, yeah, it was embarrassing. Like, I do not post content from hospitals, that is just not the vibe. My whole brand is about having fun, living your best life, and suddenly there are like, IVs involved? That's not — that's not me. That's not my story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your brand really matters to you. What you put out into the world — that's tied up in who you are as a person, not just what you do for work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Like, people get it so twisted — I'm not some sad girl drowning her sorrows or whatever. I'm out there, I'm living, I'm making content people actually enjoy. Drinking is just... it's social. It's what we do. It's literally part of my job to be at these events and show up and be fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Walk me through a typical week — what does 'showing up' actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I mean, there's always something. Monday might be a brand launch, Tuesday some PR dinner, Thursday through Sunday is kind of always going. Like it doesn't stop. And I need to be there, I need to be on. If I'm not showing up, someone else is, and then I'm — I fall behind. You fall off people's radar really fast in this industry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this constant pressure to always be on, always be present — and alcohol is just woven into every single one of those moments. That sounds genuinely exhausting, honestly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is exhausting sometimes, yeah. But like... everyone does it. My whole friend group, my collaborators, the brands I work with — it's just the culture. I'm not doing anything anyone else isn't doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet you're the one who ended up in the ER. Not them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I know. I've been trying really hard not to think about that too much, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What happens when you do think about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get kind of... I don't know. Scared, maybe? Like I'm 33 and I have this whole life that looks amazing from the outside — my DMs are full of people saying they want my life — and I'm sitting in a hospital bed at 2am and I just... it doesn't fit the narrative, you know? It's not supposed to go like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That gap — between the life everyone sees and that 2am moment — that's something you're carrying around by yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't really talk about it. Obviously. You can't exactly post 'hey guys, had my stomach pumped, link in bio.' So I just kind of... move on. Keep going. That's what you do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've gotten really, really good at moving on. Keeping the surface looking good. I'm curious — when was the last time you didn't have to perform for anyone? Including yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... I genuinely don't know. Maybe like, college? Before the following, before any of this. I used to just... exist without documenting it. Just be somewhere without it meaning something. That sounds kind of nice, actually. Is that weird to say?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound weird at all. That sounds like someone who still remembers who she is underneath all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah. Maybe. I'm still not going to like, stop going out or whatever — that is not happening, let's be clear. But... I don't know. Maybe there's something to think about here. A little bit. Don't make it a thing.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus. I know this probably wasn't your idea to be here today, so I appreciate you showing up anyway. Can you tell me a little bit about what you understand about why we're talking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my parents freaked out about some stuff they found. Which is whatever. They overreacted. I don't really get why I have to be here talking to some random person about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
