utterances.text: So from your side, they blew it way out of proportion. And now you're sitting here on a call with a stranger, which probably feels pretty unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like... I don't know. It's not like I'm some addict or whatever. They found a couple bottles. That's it. Every kid does stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not some addict. Got it. I'm not here to slap a label on you, Marcus — that's not what this is. But I am curious — why hide them? If it was no big deal, why not just leave them out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because... I mean, obviously my parents would flip out. Which they did. So. That's just... that's just how parents are, it's not like — I wasn't hiding it because I thought something was wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You knew they'd react badly, so you kept it out of sight. That makes sense on the surface. Help me understand though — how long has this been going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Like... since last year, maybe? But it's not — it's not every day or anything. Just like, weekends. When stuff is... when things are stressful I guess. Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Since last year. And it picks up when things get stressful. That's actually a really honest thing to say, and I don't think you realize that. A lot of people come in here and I never get that from them. What kinds of things have been stressful?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... school I guess. And like... my parents fight a lot. My dad kind of... he's been drinking more too, so it's like — whatever. It's fine. It's not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your dad drinks more when things are hard at home. And so do you. I'm not saying that to make you feel bad — I just want to make sure you heard what you just said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah.

I heard it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That quiet right there — what's happening for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I just... I don't want to be like him. Like, that's not — I never thought about it like that before. That I'm doing the same thing he does. That's kind of... messed up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want to be like him. That matters. That's not nothing, Marcus — the fact that you can see that pattern and it bothers you, that says something real about who you are and what you want for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm 16. It's not like I'm gonna end up like him. I can just stop whenever, you know? It's different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me be straight with you because I think you can handle it. He probably thought that too when he was 16. I'm not saying that's your future — I genuinely don't know. But "I can stop whenever" is worth actually testing. Have you tried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
I... no. Not really. I mean last month I went like two weeks without it and then my parents had a huge fight and I just... yeah.

Okay. Maybe I haven't tried that hard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You didn't want to come today, and you still showed up. You've been carrying a lot — a stressed home, your dad's drinking, school — and you found something that took the edge off. You're not stupid, you saw the pattern yourself just now without me pointing it out. And underneath all of that, you're scared of turning into something you don't want to be. That tells me there's a part of you that already knows what you want. What do you think a next step looks like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
I don't know. Maybe... maybe actually talking to someone. Like, actually talking. Not just because my parents made me.

Maybe I could come back next week or whatever. If that's — yeah.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making the time today, especially doing this from home — sometimes that's actually easier. So, what's been going on that made you want to reach out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know. My, uh... my buddy at work kind of pushed me into this. Said I looked like hell. Which, fair enough, I guess. I've been drinking more than I probably should, after everything that's happened. The divorce and... yeah. But I'm not like, an alcoholic or anything. I just — it's been a rough few months.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four months of rough is a long time to be carrying something. And it sounds like part of you knows the drinking has crept up, even if you're not sure what to make of it yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Yeah, it has. Look, she blindsided me, okay? Fifteen years and she just — out of nowhere. Well, not out of nowhere, she had a whole list, apparently. But from where I was standing it felt like out of nowhere. So yeah, I've been having a few drinks at night. Sue me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of thing — feeling blindsided by someone you built a life with — that can knock the ground right out from under a person. What's a typical night look like for you these days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home, the house is just... quiet. The kids are at her place most of the week now, so it's just me. I'll have a beer while I'm making dinner, then a couple more after. Maybe some whiskey. I'm not like, blacking out or whatever. I'm just — I don't know how else to turn my brain off. I keep going over it. All of it. What I said, what she said, what I should've said.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That loop in your head — replaying it all — that sounds exhausting. And lonely. Coming home to that quiet every night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah.

I didn't think it would be like this. I figured, you know, we'd both move on, be adults about it. But my son — he's twelve — he called me last week and I could hear in his voice that he was... I don't know. He sounded different. Like he was being careful with me. A twelve-year-old shouldn't have to be careful with his dad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment with your son — that clearly hit you in a different way than all the other stuff. That's a man who cares deeply about what kind of father he is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want him to... I don't want him to look back and think his dad fell apart. You know? That's actually — honestly, that's why I called. Not because of Kevin at work. It was that phone call. I hung up and I had a glass of whiskey in my hand and I just kind of looked at it and thought, what the hell am I doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So something shifted in that moment. It stopped being just about getting through the night and started being about something bigger — what your kids see, who you are to them through all this. What does that look like to you, being the dad you want to be right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I'm there when I have them. I'm not drinking in front of them, I want to be clear about that. But I think... I think I've been so angry at her that I haven't really let myself just — be sad about it. Like, it's easier to be pissed off than to actually sit with... with the fact that my family isn't together anymore. That that's just... done.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The anger keeps you moving. The grief... that's the thing that might actually stop you in your tracks.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
Yeah. Yeah, that's... huh.

I haven't really said that out loud before. To anyone. My brothers just, they keep telling me I'm better off, she was never right for me, blah blah blah. And maybe they're trying to help but it just makes me feel like — like nobody's letting me actually be... I don't know. Sad about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been surrounded by people trying to fast-forward you past it. And so you've been handling it alone, at night, with a drink. That actually makes a lot of sense as a coping strategy — it just has a cost.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
Yeah and the cost is my kid sounding like he's walking on eggshells.

And honestly the cost is... I wake up feeling like garbage every morning, and then I'm useless till about noon. That's not — I'm 48. I can't keep doing that. My body's not 25 anymore, like I used to bounce back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, see if I've got it right. You came into this not totally sure you had a problem — and part of you still bristles at that word. But you've also named a lot tonight: the quiet house, the loop in your head, your son's voice on that phone call, waking up feeling like garbage. Underneath the anger at your ex, there's real grief that hasn't had anywhere to go. And you're starting to wonder if the drinking is filling that space — and what it might be costing you with your kids.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

That's pretty much it, yeah.

I don't — I'm not ready to say I need to quit forever or go to rehab or whatever. But I think I need to... do something different. Because what I'm doing isn't working. It's just making me feel worse and I still wake up and the divorce is still real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to have the whole answer today. You just have to be willing to keep looking at it — which you've already done more of in the last forty minutes than it sounds like you've done in four months. What would feel like a manageable first step, even a small one, before we talk again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I don't know, try not drinking on weeknights? See if I can actually do that. And maybe actually call my son back instead of waiting for him to call me. I've been avoiding it because I don't know what to say but... he probably just wants to hear his dad sounds okay.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in... please, take your time. There's no rush here at all. I'm Sarah. I'm glad you came in today — and I mean that. Can you tell me a little bit about what brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I'll be honest with you — I did not want to come. My husband made it very clear that if I didn't... well. So here I am. I don't even know what I'm supposed to say to you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: He gave you an ultimatum. And part of you is angry about being here. That makes complete sense to me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Angry. Yes. Very. Fifty-three years we've been married and now he's — threatening to leave me like I'm some kind of... I am in pain every single day. Every. Single. Day. He doesn't understand what that is like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fifty-three years. That's a long time, and it's clear he matters to you — even if right now that's all mixed up with feeling really hurt. I want to understand... what is it like, living in that pain every day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you think it's like? I can't sleep. I used to garden. I used to walk my granddaughter to school. Now some days I can barely get out of the chair. The pills they give me barely touch it. So yes, I have a drink or two. It takes the edge off. Is that such a crime?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found something — the only thing, really — that gives you a little relief from pain that almost nothing else has touched. And you've been doing that alone. ... You started to say something a moment ago and stopped yourself. What was that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... the doctors, they throw pills at you and send you on your way. Nobody actually sits down and — nobody asks how you're doing. Not really. You're the first person who's... well. Doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It does matter. Please — what were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't want to be a burden. That's all. My daughter, my husband — they have their own lives. I've tried so hard not to make this their problem. And now I've gone and made everything worse, haven't I. This whole... situation. I've made everything worse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying so much — the pain, trying to shield everyone around you from it — and somewhere in there you found a way to get through the day that is now... causing its own kind of worry. That's a very lonely place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I knew the bottle said don't mix with alcohol. I'm not stupid. But I'm 72 years old. I thought, what's it really going to do. I just wanted... one hour. One hour without hurting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One hour of relief. That's not asking for too much. That is a deeply human thing to want. ... And you've been managing this — quietly, by yourself — for how long now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Two years. Maybe a little more. Since the hip surgery that didn't... it didn't take right. I started having a glass of wine at night and then it was... I don't know when it became more than that. I look at the bottles sometimes and I think — when did this happen to me?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When did this happen to me. ... I'm going to sit with that for a moment, if that's okay. Because I think that might be the most important thing you've said today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was always the one who had it together. Church, the grandkids, volunteering... I don't recognize myself anymore. And I think — I think I've been scared to tell anyone how bad it really is. Because then it's real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold all of this for a moment and reflect it back to you. You came in today not wanting to be here — and I respect that you came anyway. You've been living with pain that the people who were supposed to help you haven't been able to answer. You've been working so hard to protect everyone around you from that truth. And quietly, you've been asking yourself: when did this happen? And maybe — is there another way? ... What would it mean to you if things could feel even a little bit different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My granddaughter... she's seven. She keeps asking me to bake cookies with her. And I keep saying maybe next week. ... I don't want to keep saying next week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That little girl wants to bake cookies with her grandmother. And you want to be there for that. Really there. ... I don't think you're someone who gives up. I think you're someone who has been surviving — and who is sitting here today wondering if there might be more than just surviving.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know what that looks like yet. But... yes. I think I'm ready to try to figure it out. I don't want Harold to leave. And I don't want to miss any more cookies.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back. It takes something to walk through that door again, especially after a hard week. How are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. I mean... I don't even really know why I'm here. Last week was just — it was a lot. I had three shifts in a row and I just... yeah. I drank more than I wanted to. I know that's probably what you're waiting to hear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three shifts back to back, and you're still carrying all of that weight into this room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And look, I know what it looks like. But it wasn't like I was sitting there doing shots for fun. I came home at 2am after a really bad shift and I just... I didn't see another option. I tried tea, I tried TV, none of it works. The only thing that actually quiets everything down is a drink. Or three.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you've actually tried other things, and they haven't touched what you're dealing with after those shifts.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I'm so sick of people acting like a bubble bath is going to fix watching someone bleed out. Like, I'm sorry, but no. That's not — I'm not some desk job person who had a stressful meeting. I hold people's lives in my hands and then I'm just supposed to go home and do deep breathing? It's insulting, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like the advice you get doesn't come close to matching the reality of what you actually go through. That the gap between what people suggest and what your nights actually look like is just... enormous.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. God, yes. And nobody at work says anything because half of them are doing the same thing, okay? I'm not even the worst one on my unit. At least I show up. At least I'm functional. I do my job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say you're functional — I want to make sure I understand what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean I... I show up. I do my assessments. I haven't made a mistake. That I know of. ...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That pause — "that I know of" — it seems like there's something sitting in that space.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been scared. If I'm being honest. Like... there have been a couple of moments on shift where I'm just foggy, you know? And I catch myself and I think — what if I miss something? What if I'm not sharp enough and something happens to someone because of me? I think about that. I think about that a lot, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The people in your care — keeping them safe — that matters to you deeply. That's at the core of who you are as a nurse.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Of course it does. That's... that's literally why I became a nurse. I actually care about these people. Which is kind of the whole problem, right? You care too much, you absorb everything, and then you need somewhere for all of it to go, and then... god. How did I end up here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And somewhere along the way, the drinking became the place where all of that went.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It did. And I'm sitting here realizing that the thing I use to cope is now... like, it might be affecting the thing I care most about. Which is a really messed up loop to be in. I don't know. That's a messed up loop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being able to see that loop clearly — that's not easy. A lot of people can't get there. That took real honesty.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel honest. I feel... tired. And a little bit like I've been lying to myself for a while. Because I think I've known for a few months that this was getting worse. I just kept telling myself it was fine because I was still showing up. But showing up foggy isn't the same as showing up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to hold what you've shared today — you came in carrying a brutal week, feeling like no one really gets what your shifts are like. And underneath all of that frustration, there's this fear that's been growing quietly. Fear that what you're doing to cope might cost you the work you went into nursing to do. And I hear you saying you're tired of living in that fear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I can't keep walking into a shift scared of myself. That's not fair to my patients. They deserve someone who's actually present. And I used to be that person. I want to be that person again.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey. Come on in — grab a seat wherever you want. I know you've got a packed schedule so I won't keep you longer than we need. I'm just glad you showed up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... my friend basically wouldn't shut up until I came in so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's your read on why he was pushing so hard for you to come?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, he just... he gets worried about everything. Like I don't have a problem or whatever, he just overreacted. My parents are the same way, they found some bottles in my room and now it's like this whole massive — I don't know. It's not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're sitting, everyone around you kind of blew this out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Kind of. I mean... I'm sixteen, okay? Every kid does this stuff. It's not like I'm — whatever. I don't even know why I have to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got your friend on you, your parents losing their minds — that's a lot of heat coming from a lot of directions at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... yeah. It's a lot. Like I didn't even — I don't know. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it feel like to have all of that coming at you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Like, suffocating. Like everyone's watching me now and I can't — there's no room to breathe. It's annoying. I'm fine though.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Like you lost all your breathing room. Everyone's got eyes on you and there's nowhere to just... be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly that. Like before all this it was — it was the one thing that actually helped me chill out, you know? And now even that's this whole dramatic thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The one thing that helped you chill out — what was it giving you a break from?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... school's been really hard this year. Like not just grades. Just... there's a lot going on at home too. My parents fight. Like a lot. And I just... when I drank it got quiet. Everything just got quiet and I didn't have to think about any of it for a little while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it wasn't really about the drinking itself. It was about finding some quiet in the middle of a lot of noise — at home, at school. And that quiet actually meant something to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I guess. I never said it like that out loud before. It sounds kind of stupid when you put it that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. It sounds like you've been carrying a lot on your own for a long time, and you found the one thing that made it feel lighter, even just for a little while. That makes complete sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't want my parents thinking I'm like some messed up kid. That's not — I don't want to be that. I don't know. Maybe I actually do need to figure some stuff out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just reflect back what I'm hearing — you came in today feeling like everyone was overreacting, but underneath all of that there's real stuff. Noise at home, pressure at school, carrying it alone. And you found something that made the noise stop, even temporarily. And right now, for the first time, you're saying maybe there's something worth figuring out. That's not nothing. That's actually a big thing to say.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, I'm not like... promising anything. But... maybe. I don't know. Maybe it's worth talking about more.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab a seat wherever feels comfortable. I'm glad you made it today. I know the last few weeks probably haven't been easy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... thanks. Sorry, I'm — I don't really know how to do this. Like, I've never talked to a therapist before. I'm more of a, uh, 'figure it out alone in the library' kind of person. Which I guess didn't go great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — yeah, the library strategy has a pretty mixed track record. But you figured something out: you're here. That's not nothing. So what's on your mind coming into today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess I'm just — I'm embarrassed, honestly. My advisor pulled me aside last month and was like, 'your last two chapters read like they were written by someone else.' And she wasn't wrong. I was drunk when I wrote them. Or hungover. Or both.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a really painful moment — having someone you respect reflect back something you already knew but hadn't said out loud yet. What was going through your head when she said that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Pure shame. Like, I just wanted the floor to open up. But also — I kept thinking, well, at least I'm still showing up. Right? Like, I didn't miss any meetings or anything, I just... the quality wasn't there. I don't know, maybe I was minimizing it. I probably was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You caught yourself doing that — the minimizing. That actually takes a lot of self-awareness, especially right now when things are so raw.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I've been telling myself for five years that I'm smart enough to handle whatever's coming. And drinking was just... it took the edge off the noise in my head. The constant 'you don't belong here, everyone else gets it and you don't.' And then the noise got louder and I needed more to quiet it and... yeah. That's kind of how I got here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That cycle you're describing — using alcohol to silence the imposter syndrome voice, and the voice coming back louder — what does it feel like to be on the other side of that now, after detox?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terrifying. Like... the voice is still there, you know? It didn't go anywhere. And now I don't have the thing I was using to mute it. I keep thinking — what if I can't write without it? What if the last five years of work just falls apart because I'm too in my head sober?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is worried that sobriety itself might cost you the thing that matters most — your work, your research. Like the alcohol was scaffolding, and now you're not sure the building can stand on its own.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly that. Which sounds insane when I say it out loud. Like, I know intellectually that's not how it works. But it's what it feels like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound insane at all — it sounds like someone who built a coping system under enormous pressure and is now grieving it, even while knowing it was hurting them. Can I ask — what drew you to your research in the first place? Before the stress, before any of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... god, that feels like a long time ago. I wanted to work on NLP for low-resource languages. There are thousands of languages just dying out and nobody's building tools for them because there's no commercial incentive. I thought I could actually do something that mattered. I still... I still think it matters.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That passion is still right there — I can hear it in your voice. That's not gone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know. And that's kind of the worst part — I can still see what I was trying to do. It's not like I stopped caring. I just... I got buried and I didn't know how to ask for help. I didn't even know who to ask.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're asking now, though. And you made it through detox — that's genuinely hard. If the version of you who first started that research could see you sitting here today, what do you think he'd say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He'd probably say... about time, man. He'd be kind of annoyed I let it get this far. But he'd also — yeah, I think he'd be glad I'm here. I'm glad I'm here. I think. I mean, I want to finish this. I actually want to finish it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing today: you came in carrying a lot of shame, but underneath that is someone who hasn't lost sight of why his work matters. You caught yourself minimizing, you named the cycle clearly, you got through something genuinely hard this past week — and you still want to finish. That's a lot to bring into a first session. We've got room to build on that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, that's — hearing it all together like that is kind of a lot. But in a good way, I think? Like, I don't feel like a complete disaster right now. That's new.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab whatever seat works for you. I'm Marcus. Don't worry about the pile of folders, that's, uh, organized chaos. So... walk-in today, yeah? What brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... I'm here because — look, honestly? I had to come. Court said I needed to do some kind of counseling after... there was an incident. With drinking. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ah, the court-mandated shuffle. I know it well. For what it's worth, you'd be surprised how many people I've seen who started here because they had to and... ended up getting something real out of it. Not everyone, but some. What was the incident, if you don't mind me asking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: DUI. Third one. Which, I know how that sounds, but like — I'm not some... I'm not an alcoholic. I just, I had a rough few months and I made some bad calls. It's not like I drink every day or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you. And hey — you showed up. That actually means something, especially when you didn't want to be here. A lot of people just no-show and deal with the consequences later.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I figured it's better than a warrant. But I've done therapy before. Didn't really do anything for me. So I'm not, like, expecting miracles.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. No miracles promised — I'm fresh out. Can I ask, what was it like before? The therapy that didn't work. What felt off about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was like... the guy just kept asking me how things made me feel. And I'd answer and he'd write stuff down and nod, and I never felt like anything was actually happening, you know? I went like eight times and stopped. Felt like talking to a wall that had a clipboard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The clipboard wall, yeah. I get it. So nothing really connected. You mentioned the rough few months — sounds like drinking has been kind of... filling a gap for you somewhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I mean. I've got depression, officially, like diagnosed. And when it gets bad — and it's been pretty bad — drinking is the only thing that actually... it quiets everything down. Meds don't work the same way. I know that's not what you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No, that's exactly what I want to hear. That's real. Depression is loud — it's like having a bad roommate in your own head that you can't evict. And if alcohol turns that volume down, even for a few hours, I understand why you keep reaching for it. What I'm curious about is... what does it cost you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... obviously the legal stuff. Three DUIs, that's not... that's a lot. My sister won't let me see my nephew anymore. And I wake up some mornings and I just — I feel worse than before I drank, which doesn't make sense because I thought it was supposed to help.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot of losses. The legal stuff, your sister, your nephew... and you're also noticing the drinking isn't even doing the job it used to. If things were different — not perfect, just different — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I think I'd want to see my nephew again. He's six. He used to call me every Sunday. Now it's just... nothing. And I think I'd want to wake up in the morning and not already be calculating when I can have a drink. That's kind of exhausting, actually. I didn't really say that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took guts to say. Seriously. And notice what you just did — you named something real without me dragging it out of you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess... I don't know. I've been kind of on autopilot for a while. Like I stopped actually thinking about what I wanted a long time ago. It was just... get through the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just pull together what I'm hearing. You came in today because you had to — and you're clear about that, no pretending. You've had therapy before that felt hollow. You're dealing with depression that's been pretty relentless, and drinking has been a way to cope with that, even though it's started costing you things that actually matter — your nephew, your mornings, your freedom. And somewhere underneath all of that, there's a guy who still wants something different. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that tracks. I didn't think I'd be saying that after like forty minutes but... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what do you want to do with that? Not what the court wants, not what your sister wants — what do you want to do with what you just figured out today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I want to come back. Which I wasn't expecting to say. I'm not making any big promises or whatever, but I think I could — maybe. Try this for real this time.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab a seat wherever. I promise I won't keep you past your next class. Well, probably. I'm known to run long when someone's interesting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Thanks. I only have like forty minutes so — yeah. I'm here. My friend Carol basically shoved me through the door, but... I don't know. Maybe it's time to actually talk to somebody. Or maybe I'm just doing this so she'll stop calling me every day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Forty minutes is plenty. And hey — showing up when someone else nudged you still counts as showing up. That took something. What's been going on for you lately, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, Carol seems to think I have a... drinking problem. Which, I mean, I've been drinking more than usual, I'll admit that. But I lost my husband eight months ago, so — I think most people would do the same thing? Like, it's not like I'm doing anything crazy. I still go to work. I still function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eight months. That's so recent. Thirty-one years together and then... just quiet. The drinking makes sense as a way to get through nights that might otherwise feel completely unlivable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. It takes the edge off — at night especially. The house is just so... *sighs* ...it's a lot. But I'm not falling apart. I make dinner, I go to my job, I do what needs doing. It's just a phase, you know? They say the first year is the hardest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does a regular day actually look like for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I go to work, come home, sometimes make dinner, watch TV. Have some wine. Go to bed. I mean — I used to have a whole life. Book club, dinners, Tom and I had friends over all the time. Now I just... people look at me like I'm about to shatter, and I can't deal with it. It's easier to just be by myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're holding it together at work, managing everyone else's grief about your grief, coming home to silence, and doing it all over again. That's genuinely exhausting. You're carrying way more than most people could.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't have a choice, do I? My kids have their own lives, they're far away, I'm not going to make this their problem. I just have to get through it. And I will. It's just — *waves hand* — it's just a hard time. The drinking is fine. It's temporary.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is really hoping that's true — that there's a finish line somewhere around the one-year mark. And another part of you... I wonder if that part is why you're sitting in this chair right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... *long pause* ...okay. If I'm being honest. Last Tuesday I woke up and I didn't — I couldn't really remember the end of the night. And that scared me. That's not... I've never been that person. I don't want to be that person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds frightening — losing time like that. Can I ask you something totally different? What do you miss most? Not about drinking or not drinking. About your life before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: *voice cracks* Tom used to make the worst puns. Just absolutely terrible. And I'd groan, and he'd laugh at himself, and I'd laugh at him laughing... *pause* ...I haven't laughed like that since he died. I don't know how to be this person. I'm fifty-five years old and I don't know how to be alone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't just miss him — you miss who you were when you were with him. The woman who laughed at terrible puns.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: *crying softly* Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. And the drinking... it doesn't actually help. I know that. It just turns the volume down for a few hours and then I wake up and everything's still there, and now I feel worse on top of it. I know. I just — I don't know what else to do with myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you just said something really important? You came in today — even pushed through the door — because part of you already knew. You know the drinking is just turning down the volume, not healing anything. You're grieving one of the great loves of your life, you've pulled away from everyone, and last Tuesday scared you. And underneath all of that... you're not ready to give up on feeling like yourself again. The woman with the terrible-pun-laughing husband.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... *sniffles* ...yeah. Yeah, that's right. I'm fifty-five, not dead. Tom would be furious with me, honestly. He'd say something completely corny like — *small laugh* — 'You're a lot of work, Margaret, but you're worth it.' He was always better at this stuff than I was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: He sounds like he was pretty great. What do you think he'd actually want you to do next — not in a guilt-trippy way, I'm genuinely asking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He'd say call your sister. He always liked my sister better than I did, honestly. *laughs a little* And he'd want me back at book club. And... talking to someone. Professionally. Which I guess is what I'm doing right now. Can we — is this something we can keep doing? Is that how this works?

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Reyes — and before you ask, no, this isn't the part where I make you sit in a circle and say your name. You can just... sit wherever feels least uncomfortable. How're you doing after last night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm fine. I mean — I'm not fine, obviously, I just got out of the ER, but like... I don't need to be here. They made it sound like I had some big problem and I just, I hadn't eaten, okay? It was a stupid thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, getting sent somewhere you didn't ask to go — that's a whole thing. I'd be annoyed too. So tell me a little about yourself, though, because I'm realizing I don't know anything about you except what's on this intake form, which says basically nothing useful.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm an artist. Painter, mostly. And before you say anything — I know what this looks like, right? The tortured artist clichÃ©, drinking to create or whatever. But it's not like that. Alcohol actually... it loosens something. It always has. I've been doing it for years and it works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's been a real part of your process — not just habit, but something that genuinely felt like it was unlocking something for you creatively.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Everyone acts like I'm delusional but there's actual... like, Pollock, Basquiat, basically every artist people actually give a damn about — they weren't drinking green juice, you know? There's a reason. It lowers the filter. And I need that. My brain is just too... critical when I'm sober. Everything I make looks wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That inner critic — sounds like it can be brutal. And you found something that quieted it. That makes a lot of sense, actually. Can I ask you something though? You said the work has been going well... is that still true?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I mean... it's going. I've been working. I'm always working. It's just — okay, fine, the last few pieces haven't been what I wanted them to be, but that happens. Every artist has dry spells. That has nothing to do with drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're still putting in the hours, still showing up to the canvas — that's not nothing. And at the same time, something about the recent work isn't landing the way you want it to. What does that feel like, when you look at it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It feels like... someone else made it. Like there's no — I don't know. There used to be this thing in my work, this tension, and now it's just... muddy. Everything looks muddy. I thought I was just tired but it's been like eight months of muddy and I don't... I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eight months of muddy. That's a long time to feel disconnected from the thing that matters most to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It really is. And I keep drinking more thinking it'll click back into place, and it just... doesn't. Which is — I mean, that's frustrating. That's really frustrating because it always worked before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've actually been trying to solve the problem — using the same tool you've always trusted, pushing harder — and instead of getting the clarity back, it's like the tool is... doing something different now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — huh. That's a weird way to think about it but... yeah. It's not working the same way. And I've been pretending it is, but honestly... I can't remember the last time I finished something I was actually proud of.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here's something that might be useful to know — and tell me if you want me to skip the science part. Alcohol does lower inhibition at first, which is real. But with daily use over time, it actually starts to dull the prefrontal cortex in ways that make fine creative judgment harder. The thing that felt like it was silencing your inner critic? It may be silencing the part of you that knows what good work looks like too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So you're saying... the thing I thought was helping me... has been making my work worse? For how long?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's genuinely hard to sit with. And the fact that you're even asking that question — not defending it, actually asking — says something about how much you care about your art. That takes courage.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't feel courageous. I feel kind of stupid, honestly. Like, what if — what if I get sober and I still can't make good work? What if the alcohol wasn't the problem and I'm just... not as good as I thought I was? That's a terrifying thing to consider.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this real fear underneath — not just about drinking, but about identity. About what it would mean if the art you've made for years wasn't fully yours, or wasn't your best. And also, what it would mean to find out the other side. You've spent years telling yourself one story about how you create. And now you're sitting here, just barely considering that there might be a different one. That's not stupid — that's one of the bravest things a person can do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I really miss liking my own work. I used to love what I made. I want that back. I don't know if I can do this but I... I want that back.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this probably wasn't something you had on your calendar this week. Take your time getting settled — there's no agenda here, no checklist we have to get through. I just want to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I didn't really have a choice, did I? HR made it pretty clear this was... mandatory. So here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like you were pushed into this room. What's your own understanding of why they sent you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was an... incident, they're calling it. My colleague — Sandra — she went to the principal because she said I seemed off one morning. Which is just... I had a cold. I was fighting something off. And somehow that becomes a whole HR situation.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You had a cold, and it turned into this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I have been teaching for eleven years. Eleven years, no write-ups, no complaints from parents, nothing. And one morning I'm under the weather and suddenly I'm being — evaluated. Like I'm some kind of liability. It's insulting, honestly. It's insulting to everything I've put into that school.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eleven years of showing up, doing the work, caring about those kids. That's real, and I hear you — this feels completely out of proportion to what happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. It does. I'm not — I'm not the kind of teacher who just phones it in. Those are my kids in there. I know their names, I know which ones are struggling at home. I give a damn.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I believe that. Can I ask — when Sandra pulled you aside, what was that actually like for you in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... humiliating. She was trying to be kind about it, I guess. She said she was concerned. But I just — my first reaction was, who does she think she is? She doesn't know what my evenings are like. She doesn't know what I'm carrying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What your evenings are like...

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I — yeah. It's been a hard year. My wife and I are... things are rocky. And after a full day of managing twenty-eight twelve-year-olds, I just need to decompress. So I have a couple drinks when I get home. That's not... that's not a crime. A lot of people do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A couple drinks to take the edge off after everything piles up. What does a typical evening actually look like — walk me through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home around four-thirty. I'll have a beer while I'm making dinner. Maybe another one after. And then... I don't know, sometimes if it's been a really rough day I'll have a whiskey before bed. Helps me sleep. Without it I just — I lie there and my brain won't stop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing. You're carrying real stress — a hard year at home, a demanding job you clearly take seriously — and somewhere along the way drinking became how you get through the night and fall asleep. And now you're here feeling like this whole thing is unfair. And yet... you also said something a minute ago that I want to sit with. You said Sandra doesn't know what your evenings are like. That's not the same as saying there's nothing to know.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay. Yeah. Sometimes I wonder if I'm relying on it more than I used to. Like... in the mornings, I'm not always — I notice I'm not at my best. And I'm aware of that. I don't want my students to see me like that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want your students to see you like that. What does it mean to you that that still matters so much?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means I still... I still give a damn. About who I am. I just — I don't know how I got here, you know? Like I didn't set out to be the guy who needs a drink to get through the night. That's not who I thought I was. That's not the person I wanted to be when I started teaching.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't set out to be here. And something in you is noticing the gap — between the person you want to be and what's actually been happening. Saying that out loud, in here, for the first time? That takes more honesty than most people give themselves credit for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I guess it does. I still don't know what I'm supposed to do about any of this, but... yeah. I hear what you're saying.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know it's not always easy to walk through that door. What brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... I saw something on the VA website, I don't know. My husband kept sending me these links and I finally just... I don't even really know why I'm here, honestly. I've never done the therapy thing. I'm more of a just push through it kind of person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something made you push through that door today, though. Even if you can't quite put a name to it yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. It's probably nothing, I think I'm just tired. I have a four-month-old, so. You know how it is. Or maybe you don't. It's just — everyone drinks wine to wind down, right? It's not like I'm... I don't know. My husband just worries about everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The tiredness sounds real. Four months in is... it's its own kind of relentless. What does a typical evening look like for you, after the baby goes down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay so she goes down around seven-thirty if we're lucky, and then I just... I pour a glass of wine. Sometimes two. And I sit on the couch and I just don't move for like an hour and I don't think about anything and it's the only time all day that I feel like — like I can breathe. And then I do it again the next night. And the night after that. It's been like four months of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four months of holding everything together and that one hour is the only place you get to just... stop. That makes a lot of sense. It's been doing something important for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It's like my off switch. But... I don't know, lately I've been waking up at three in the morning and my heart is just — it's racing and I feel kind of gross? And she cries and I get up and I'm fine, I'm totally fine, but there's this part of me that's like... is this okay? Am I okay?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something in you is asking that question. And you came here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I keep thinking about her, like when she's older. When she can actually remember things. I don't want her to remember me as the mom who always had a glass of wine in her hand, you know? My mom was... it doesn't matter. I just — I don't want to be that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image of who you want to be for her — can you tell me more about that? What does that mom look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's... present. Like actually there. Not just in the room but actually there. I want her to be able to come to me with stuff and know that I'm going to be — solid. That I'm not going to be checked out or fuzzy or whatever. I want to be the kind of mom she remembers as steady. God, that sounds so cheesy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound cheesy at all. It sounds like you know exactly who you want to be. And right now there's this gap between that person and the nightly wine that's helping you survive — and you're sitting right in the middle of that gap, feeling it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I never said it like that but yeah. It's like I need it to get through the day but it's also the thing that's kind of in the way. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense. So let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You're exhausted in a way that goes bone-deep. You found something that turns the noise off, and it works — until three in the morning when your body's telling you something different. And underneath all of it is this woman who wants to be fully there for her daughter, the way maybe she didn't always have someone be there for her. And that matters to you more than almost anything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. Yeah, all of that. Wow.

Okay so what do I do? Like, I'm not — I don't want to just white-knuckle it. I tried that for a week and I was a disaster. But maybe there's something else? I don't know what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I love that you're already thinking about what else is possible. What's one small thing — and it doesn't have to be perfect — that you've ever done that gave you that same off-switch feeling? Even for a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Baths. Before the baby I used to take these long hot baths and just... zone out. I haven't done that in forever. And like, I used to run, but that feels like a different lifetime. Maybe I could start with just... I don't know, doing that? And maybe not pouring the glass the second she goes down. Just like, wait. See what happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here not knowing why, and in less than an hour you've named what's driving all of this, what you want instead, and already started figuring out a different path. That's not nothing. That's actually you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
I wasn't expecting to feel like this after. Like... lighter, kind of. I thought you were just going to tell me I have a problem and hand me a pamphlet.

Can I come back?

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this wasn't exactly your call, so I appreciate you being here regardless. I'm Marcus — you can skip the formal stuff. Before anything else, can you just tell me in your own words what brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My sister basically dragged me here. Like, I love her, but... I don't know. I'm fine. I work nights, I bartend — everyone who does this job drinks after a shift. That's just kind of how it goes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been bartending for a while — what's that lifestyle actually like, day to day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... you're on your feet for eight hours, people are yelling at you, you're managing a whole crowd, and by the end of the night your brain is just fried. So yeah, you have a few drinks to come down. That's not a disorder, that's just Tuesday. Everyone on my crew does it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's a high-pressure job and the drinks help you land after a shift. I get that. So what did your sister actually say to you — what was it that worried her enough to bring you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said she can't remember the last time she saw me sober. Which is — okay, that's just dramatic. She sees me in the mornings sometimes, and yeah maybe I'm a little rough, but I'm not like... stumbling around. And then she brought up how I snapped at her last week and made it this whole thing. I was hungover, I apologized, it's done.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a heavy thing for someone who loves you to say.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It pissed me off, honestly. Because I'm functioning. I show up to work, I pay my rent, I'm not — I'm not some guy passed out in a parking lot. I just drink after work like a normal person who has a stressful job. I don't understand why that's suddenly this big emergency.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're keeping it together — work, bills, showing up. I hear that. But I want to ask you something, and I want you to be honest with yourself, not with me. When your sister said she couldn't remember the last time she saw you sober... what actually went through your head in that moment? Not what you said back to her — what you thought.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I got defensive. Obviously. But then later — like 3am, couldn't sleep — I was actually trying to think of when that was. The last day I didn't drink. And I couldn't come up with one. Not like last week, not last month... I don't know. And that kind of, um. Yeah. That got to me a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That question kept you up at 3am.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I hate that it did, because I've always been the one who has it together in my family, you know? Like, I'm the one people call when stuff goes wrong. And now I'm lying there trying to think of one sober day and I can't. I genuinely cannot answer that question and that's... that's a weird feeling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you if the answer turns out to be a really long time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... it means maybe I'm not as in control of this as I thought I was. Which is weird to say out loud. It's not like I'm blackout every night — I mean, sometimes, but mostly I just need a couple to come down, and then a couple more, and I've been doing it so long I don't even think about it. It's just... what I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what you've been telling me. You came in because your sister pushed you to, and at first that felt unfair — because by your measure, you're functioning. Showing up. Paying bills. That's always been the bar for okay. But then at 3am the question landed: when was the last sober day? And you couldn't find one. And sitting here now, you're starting to wonder whether drinking every night is actually a choice you're making, or just something that's running on autopilot without you ever deciding it should.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I never sat down and decided to be this guy. It just kind of happened while I was busy working.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If nothing changes — if things stay exactly as they are right now — what does your life look like a year from today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? More of the same. Maybe worse. I work in a bar, I see the regulars — guys who've been planted on the same stool for twenty years. I always told myself I wasn't like them. But... I don't know anymore. Maybe that's the direction I'm going. And that's not — that's not what I want. That's not who I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something important — that's not who you want to be. And the fact that you sat here and actually let yourself go to that honest place, instead of just running out the clock until I stopped asking questions... that's not nothing. You didn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm still not ready to say I have like, a capital-P Problem. But I think I need to find out if I can even stop for a day. Just one day. To see if I can. Because right now, honestly, I don't know if I can. And that's kind of freaking me out.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, I'm glad you made it in today. I know it wasn't the easiest morning... How have you been since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my mom literally drove me here so. Not like I had a choice. But yeah, it's been rough, I guess. I don't really know how to explain it. Just... a lot going on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like things have been heavy. Like you're carrying something you're not quite sure how to put into words.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... everything felt like it was starting to get better and then last weekend happened and now everyone's acting like I'm some kind of... like I have this huge problem or something. I had a few drinks at my buddy's place. That's it. I don't see why that's suddenly this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels really unfair - like you were making progress, and then one night out becomes proof of something bigger in everybody else's eyes.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And like... I don't know. Maybe they're right, I don't know. I just... nothing I do is ever going to be enough for them. I could quit entirely and they'd still be watching me like I'm about to screw up. What's even the point of trying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds really exhausting... feeling like no matter what you do, it's never going to be enough. Like the finish line keeps moving.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is exhausting. I've actually been trying. Like, genuinely. And then one weekend and it's just... forget it. It doesn't matter what I do. It's like I'm already the screw-up in everyone's head and I can't change that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been trying. And I want to make sure that doesn't get lost here... What did that effort actually look like for you over the past few weeks?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I didn't drink for like two weeks. Which... I don't know, I've never really done that before in college. I went to class. Called my mom back when she texted. And then... I don't know. Saturday happened and it's like, I'm just not built for this kind of change. Some people are just wired a certain way, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two weeks without drinking - that's not a small thing. That took real effort. And I'm also hearing something underneath that... like a part of you that's not sure if change is actually possible for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. Like my friends all drink. That's just what we do on weekends, that's our thing. I'm not gonna be the weird one sitting there with a Sprite while everyone else is having a good time. That's not... that's not the life I want. So what, I just never have fun again?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So belonging - being part of your crew, not feeling like the odd one out - that really matters to you. That's something you genuinely value.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, of course it does. But also... I don't know. I had this moment last week where I was sitting in my car after practice and I just... I sat there for like twenty minutes just thinking. About stuff. About where things are going. I don't usually do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment in your car... what was going through your mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... I was thinking about five years from now. Like, where do I actually want to be. And my dad... my dad drinks, has for as long as I can remember. And I've always said, like, I'm never gonna be like that. That's not me. And I just sat there wondering if... I don't know. If that's already what's happening. Maybe not. I'm only 21. Maybe I still have time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a part of you that's holding onto that - the belief that you still have time. That you can still become someone different from what you're afraid of.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, I think so. I mean, I'm not him. I know that. And the fact that I'm even thinking about it has to mean something, right? Like... I still have a shot at this. I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It means a lot, actually. You walked through that door today. You went two weeks making real changes. You had a hard weekend and you're still sitting here, still thinking about who you want to be. That's not someone who's given up - that's someone who hasn't stopped fighting, even when it doesn't feel that way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I mean, I still think everyone's being way too dramatic about it, I want to be clear about that. But... maybe there's something worth figuring out here. I'm not saying I have a problem. I'm just saying... I don't know. I'll keep coming in. We can keep talking.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time for this. I know this probably wasn't how you were planning to spend your afternoon. I'm Marcus — we can just talk, no agenda, no checklist. What's on your mind coming in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think this whole thing is... look, I'm here because I was told I basically had to be. That's it. I don't think I need to be talking to anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't choose this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And it's — I've been teaching for eleven years. Eleven years, no problems, and suddenly because Janet decides to play concerned colleague or whatever, now I'm in therapy. It's insulting, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would you want me to know about what actually happened — from your side of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What happened is I had a rough night, I came in a little tired, and she thought she smelled something. Which — I had a drink or two the night before, okay? That's not... I mean, I'm a grown adult. That's legal. That's my business. And she goes straight to the principal instead of just talking to me like a person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've spent over a decade showing up for those kids every single day. That's not nothing. And I can hear how much this feels like a betrayal — from someone you actually trusted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it does. I mean... we eat lunch together. We've covered each other's classes. And she just — yeah. [pause] Whatever. I don't really want to talk about Janet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm curious about something different then — what does a typical evening look like for you, after you get home from school?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... normal stuff. I get home, I decompress. Teaching middle schoolers is — you have no idea. It's exhausting. So I pour myself a drink, watch something, unwind. That's it. That's the whole big scandal apparently.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like those evenings are pretty essential — like a pressure valve after days that take a real toll on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly, yes. Thank you. It's not like I'm — I'm not sitting there with a bottle in a paper bag, okay? I have wine. Sometimes a couple glasses, sometimes... I don't know, more. But it's not a problem. I know what a problem looks like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think she actually saw that morning — what was it, from her side, that worried her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. [long pause] I guess there was one day a few weeks back where I was really dragging. Like, not just tired-tired. And I probably — I mean, the kids were fine. I made it through fine. But I could see how maybe from the outside... [trails off] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just check I'm following you. You came into this pretty angry — feeling reported on, misjudged, by someone you thought had your back. And then when I asked you to think about what she might have actually seen, something shifted a little. You started putting yourself in her shoes for a second. There's a version of this where you already know what she was worried about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. Maybe. I'm not ready to say she was right. But I've been really tired lately. Not just normal teacher tired. And I know the drinking has gone up this year. It's been a rough year — my dad's been sick, there's been stuff at home... it just kind of crept up on me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It crept up on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I don't — I don't want it to be a thing, you know? Like, I'm not that guy. I coach the robotics team. I write college recommendations on weekends. That's who I am. But lately it's like... I need it to get to sleep. That's new. That's not how it used to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That guy — the one who coaches robotics and writes those letters on weekends — what would it mean to him if things kept going the direction they've been going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [long pause] I don't want to lose my job. I really don't. And I don't want to... work is the only place I still feel like myself, honestly. So. I don't know what I'm saying exactly. I just — maybe I should actually be here. Maybe.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, take a seat. I'm glad you made it today. Walk-ins can feel a little strange — you're not quite sure what you're walking into. What's your name?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Harold. Um... yeah, I wasn't — I almost didn't come, honestly. Sat in the parking lot for a good twenty minutes before I got out of the car.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That says something, Harold — that you came in anyway. What was it that finally got you through the door today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor. She, uh... she told me my liver numbers were — they weren't good. Asked me flat out how much I was drinking and I told her. More than I should, I guess. She said I needed to talk to somebody. So here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She gave you some hard news, and instead of pushing it away, you're sitting here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know what I expected retirement to be like. I thought I'd be relieved, you know? Thirty-seven years with the post office and I'm finally done. But then it's just... quiet. My wife passed four years back, kids are scattered all over. The days got long. I started having a drink or two in the evenings and then — I don't know. It crept up on me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about what those long days actually feel like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Empty. That's the word. I wake up and there's nothing — no reason to get dressed, nobody expecting me anywhere. I used to have a route, people knew me. Now I'm just... I watch a lot of TV. By three o'clock I'm already thinking about that drink. It's something to look forward to, I suppose. Which sounds pathetic when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound pathetic. It sounds like someone grieving a lot of losses at once — your wife, your work, your sense of place in the world. And you're honest enough to name it. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought of it as grief. But... yeah, maybe. I kept telling myself, this is just what old guys do. Sit around, have their beers. But it's more than beer now. A bottle of wine, sometimes more. I don't sleep right, I feel foggy most mornings. I'm not — this isn't who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say 'this isn't who I am' — who is it you feel like you've lost sight of?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I used to be... active. Volunteered at the library on Saturdays. Coached little league for years when my boys were growing up. I'd go fishing with my neighbor Frank every other weekend — but he moved to Arizona two years back. I just stopped doing all of it and I can't really tell you exactly why. I just... stopped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking didn't come out of nowhere. It moved in when the things that gave you connection and purpose started disappearing — one by one.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I didn't even notice it happening. And now I'm sitting here at 65 thinking — how much time do I actually have left? And is this really how I want to spend it? My doctor scared me, but it's more than the liver thing. I don't want to just... wait around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, Harold. You retired after a long career, lost your wife, your routine fell apart, and the connections — Frank, the volunteering, little league — those slipped away too. Drinking came in to fill that space, to give the day some shape. But it's taken a toll on your health, and more than that, it doesn't feel like you. Your doctor's news was a wake-up call — not just about your liver, but about whether this is really the life you want. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. You do. And hearing it said like that... I don't know, it feels less shameful somehow. Like I'm not just weak. I just got lost.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things were genuinely different six months from now — if you'd found your footing again — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd get back to the library. Or something like it. Maybe call my son in Denver — we talk, but not really, you know what I mean? I'd like to sleep properly again. Wake up and feel like myself. Maybe not drink at all... I don't know if I can say that yet. But a lot less. Enough to feel clear in the morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Harold, you sat in that parking lot for twenty minutes and still walked through the door. In the last hour you've named what's driving this, you've talked honestly about who you want to be, and you have a clear picture of what better looks like. That's the actual work. I think you can do this — not because I'm supposed to say that, but because you already started.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wasn't expecting to feel... lighter, I guess. Thought it'd be harder to say all this out loud. Maybe I'll call Denver tonight. Start somewhere small.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you today. Last time we spoke, things were moving in a direction you felt pretty good about — I'm curious, how have things been since then?
