utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, honestly? Pretty amazing. Like, I just hit 200K on Instagram, which — I mean, that's huge for me, and my whole brand is really taking off. So, yeah. Things are great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real milestone — congratulations. And I'm glad things feel good. You also mentioned in your message last week that you'd hit a rough patch. Tell me more about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right, yeah, that. I mean... it was nothing, really. Just a bit of a blip. My friend Becca made this whole thing out of nothing at a dinner, and I just — I don't know, it kind of threw me off for a second. But I'm fine now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something Becca said got to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... she just — okay, so we were at this launch event, and I'd had a few drinks, obviously, because that's what you DO at launch events, right? And she pulled me aside and was like, 'You really need to slow down,' and I just — I felt so called out. In front of people. It was embarrassing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a very public moment — being singled out like that. What was going through your mind when she said it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't know, I kept thinking, are people talking about me? Like, is this becoming a whole narrative? Because I'm a public person, okay, and the last thing I need is some story. I've just been feeling like... like everyone's watching me differently now. It's weird. It makes me kind of paranoid, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that weight — the feeling that people see you differently — on top of everything else. And you've still shown up here, even when things got uncomfortable. That says something about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I mean — it's just frustrating, you know? Because drinking is literally part of my lifestyle content. It's what my audience follows me for. Brunch culture, nightlife, whatever. It's not like I'm hiding anything. I'm doing it on camera. So how is that suddenly a problem?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the very thing people are concerned about is also the thing that built your career. Those feel like they're completely at odds with each other.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly! Like, yes, thank you. And I'm not — look, I'm not blacking out every night, okay? I go to events, I have wine, I take cute pictures, I go home. That is my job. My doctor doesn't get it, Becca doesn't get it, nobody gets it. It's just — ugh. It's exhausting having to defend myself constantly to everyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear a lot of frustration. And I want to ask you something a little different — when you picture your life, not the brand, not the content, just... your actual life... what do you want it to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. That's kind of a heavy question. I guess I just want people to stop worrying about me? Like, I want things to go back to how they were before everyone started making it weird. Before I even had to think about any of this. It was... simpler.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's something that sounds like loss in that. Missing a time when things felt lighter.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. I had this moment last week — I was sitting alone after some event, and I was just like, when did this get so complicated? And I don't even fully know what 'this' is. Like, is it the drinking? Is it the friends? Is it just... everything? I don't know. It just made me really sad for a minute. Which is dumb.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's not dumb. Sitting with a hard question, even just for a minute — that takes something. What do you think you'd need to feel less... complicated?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think I just need people to trust me. Like, I know myself. And maybe — maybe I can be a little more intentional, like I don't need a drink at every single event. But that's my call to make. Not Becca's. Not my doctor's. Mine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're claiming ownership of this — it's your life, your choices to make. And I noticed what you said: 'a little more intentional.' That came from you, not from anyone else in this room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah. I'm not saying anything is wrong. But like — I can be intentional. I'm a very intentional person, that's literally how I built my whole brand. So. I've got this. I think I just needed to, like, talk it out a little.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. I know it's not easy walking into a place like this, especially... I imagine there's a lot going on for you right now. Can you tell me a little about what brought you here — in your own words, whatever feels okay to share?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... my sister basically made me come. She flew in from back home and she was — she was upset. I told her she's overreacting. I drink sometimes, okay? That's not a crime. A lot of people drink. I don't know why everyone is making such a big deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your sister loves you enough to fly across the world. And you showed up. Even if it wasn't entirely your choice — you're here. That means something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean... she worries too much. She doesn't understand what it's like here. Back home I had everyone around me — my cousins, my mom, my friends from school. Here it's just... I go to work, I come home. That's it. She doesn't get that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Work, then home. Work, then home. ... That sounds incredibly lonely.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it... it really is. I didn't think it would be like this when I moved. I thought, you know, new country, new start, exciting. And then I got here and I just — I didn't know anyone. I don't even know my neighbors' names. Back home you just... everyone knows everyone. Here people don't even make eye contact on the bus.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came here with hope. A vision of something better. And instead you found yourself... invisible. Like you'd lost yourself somewhere in the move.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's — yeah, that's actually exactly it. Invisible. I didn't... I never thought about it that way but that's what it feels like. Like I could disappear and nobody here would even notice. And so at night I have a few drinks and at least then I can just... turn my brain off for a bit. Stop thinking about how alone I am. Is that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No. It's not terrible. It makes complete sense that you found something that gives you relief, even for a few hours. You've been carrying something really heavy, completely on your own. ... What I'm curious about — and you don't have to answer this — is what it costs you. The drinking. Not what your sister thinks. What you notice.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I wake up feeling like garbage sometimes. And I've missed a couple of shifts. Not many. Two, maybe three. And I — okay, there was one night I called my mom at like 2am crying and I don't even really remember what I said and she was so scared and I felt so ashamed after. That was... that was not good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You heard your mom's fear. Even through the haze of that night, you felt it. And it stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's already worried about me being so far away. I don't want to give her more reasons to worry. She's not — she's not young anymore, you know? I came here to build something. To make her proud. And instead I'm... I don't know. I don't know what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you, if that's okay. You came here to build something — for yourself, for your mom. You've been surviving an enormous amount of isolation without any real support around you. And somewhere inside you there's still that person who wants to make her proud. She hasn't gone anywhere. ... You've been doing this alone for a long time. What would it mean to not have to do it alone anymore?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... honestly I don't even know what that looks like. I've tried before — I went to this one counselor last year and it was just very... clinical? Like she kept giving me worksheets. It didn't feel like she actually cared. I stopped going after four sessions. So I guess I'm a little — I don't want to waste my time again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've tried to get help before and it didn't feel real. You deserved better than worksheets. And you came back anyway — that's not nothing. That's actually kind of remarkable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if it's remarkable. My sister basically dragged me here. But... I don't know. This feels different. You're actually listening. Like you're not just waiting for me to stop talking so you can give me a handout. ... Sorry, that probably sounds rude.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize. Please. I want you to say exactly what's true for you in here. Always. ... What you just said — that this feels different — I want to stay with that for a second. What would it mean for you if you found that connection you've been missing? Not just here, but... in your life here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. I think I would feel like... like I actually live here? Right now I feel like I'm just passing through, like I'm a ghost. If I had even one real friend here. Someone I could call. I think I would drink less, honestly. I think the drinking is just because I have nothing else to do with all that... that feeling. That emptiness at night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something really important — that the drinking fills a space that loneliness carved out. You can see the connection. And you can imagine something different. A life where you actually feel present here, rooted, known by someone. That vision is real. It exists in you. I think that's where we start — not with taking something away, but with building something toward. Would you be willing to come back and keep exploring that together?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think... I think I would. I haven't felt this understood in a really long time. Maybe since before I moved. So yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey. I'm glad you came in. I know this probably wasn't your idea, so I want to be upfront with you — I'm not here to lecture you, and I don't report back to your parents about what you say in this room. My name's Dr. Reyes. This is your time. I just want to understand what's going on for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't even want to be here. Like, at all. My parents made me come, so. Can we just... get this over with? I didn't do anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like this whole thing is being done to you. Like nobody asked you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. They found some bottles in my room and just — completely lost it. Like it's this massive crisis. It's not. Kids drink. It's normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say it's normal — help me understand what you mean by that. What does drinking look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... I have a few drinks on weekends sometimes. Maybe during the week if it's been a bad week. It's not like I'm doing hard drugs or whatever. My parents are acting like I'm some kind of... I don't know. Addict or something. That's insane.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know the difference between what you're doing and other things, and that matters. I also notice you came in here ready to defend yourself — which tells me you're someone who doesn't just roll over. I can work with that. I'm guessing nobody's actually asked you your side of this yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. They just... yelled. And then grounded me. And then — this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's been going on lately — before they found the bottles? Like, what does a regular week look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's... fine. School. My parents are always on me about grades and like, what college I'm gonna go to, and I'm sixteen so that's just... a lot. I don't know. Drinking kind of helps me, like... relax. Turn my brain off for a bit. Is that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it does something for you. It quiets things down.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like, when I drink, it's just... quieter. In my head. Everything's kind of loud normally and I just... I don't know. It works. Nothing else really works like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That loudness in your head — what does it sound like when it's not quiet?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I don't know. Like... like I'm always screwing something up? Or like people are gonna figure out that I don't actually have it together. Like at school I act like everything's fine but... I don't know. That probably sounds dumb.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound dumb at all. It sounds exhausting. Performing like everything's fine when inside it's loud and you're worried people are seeing through you — that's a heavy thing to carry. And you found something that turns all of that down. Of course you'd hold onto it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean — I know it's not like, the smartest thing. I'm not stupid. But like, I've tried other stuff. Going for walks or whatever, the things people say to do. And it doesn't work. The drinking actually works. So what am I supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a part of you that already knows this isn't a perfect solution. But it's the only thing that's been working. So even thinking about stopping feels... I don't know, what does it feel like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't — I didn't say I want to stop. But... [pause] ...I don't know what I'd do. Like, what would I actually do when it gets like that. That's kind of... yeah. That kind of freaks me out actually. I never said that to anyone before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You came in here today pretty angry — you didn't choose this, and nobody asked you. You don't think you have some massive problem, and you want people to stop treating you like you do. But at the same time, there's a lot of pressure and noise in your life, and drinking has been the one thing that makes that manageable. And somewhere underneath all of that, there's a question you've maybe been avoiding — what happens if I don't have this anymore? What do I do then? And that question scares you. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. [quiet] I thought you were just gonna tell me I'm messed up. But you didn't. So... I don't know. Maybe I could actually talk about this. Like, for real. I don't know if that'll fix anything but... maybe.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you taking the time today, especially given everything on your plate. I know this wasn't exactly... a voluntary arrangement. Before we get into anything, I just want you to know — there's no agenda here. I'm not here to tell you what to do or make any judgments. I'm just here to listen. So... what's it been like, leading up to today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Annoying. I mean, no offense, but I've got a board presentation Thursday, I've got a CFO who's threatening to jump ship, and I'm sitting here doing... this. Because someone at HR decided to make a mountain out of a molehill. I'm fine. I run a two-hundred-million-dollar company. If I wasn't fine, you'd know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot riding on you right now. Board presentation, a CFO situation, and now this on top of it all. That's... that's a tremendous amount of weight to be carrying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well, that's the job. That's been the job for fifteen years. You think it gets easier? It doesn't. You just — you get better at managing it. I've always managed it. That's literally what I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real. Fifteen years of managing impossible pressure — that takes something most people genuinely don't have. And I'm curious... when you say you manage it, what does that actually look like? At the end of a day like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I — I decompress. Like anyone would. I get home, I pour a drink, I sit in my study. Read. Think through problems. It helps me... it helps me come down from the day so I can actually sleep. Without it I'd be up until three, four in the morning. The scotch is — it's a tool. A very expensive tool, but a tool.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's become something you rely on to find quiet. To turn the noise down enough to rest. ... Can I ask — and you don't have to answer this any particular way — when was the last time you felt quiet without it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. That's a... I don't — I mean, years ago, maybe. Before the Series B. Before my dad died. I used to run. I'd run and it would just... clear out. But I blew out my knee in 2019 and that was... that was that. And after Dad... I don't know. Things kind of shifted.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Things shifted when your father died. ...

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He was... he worked his whole life. Never stopped. Died at his desk, basically. Heart attack at sixty-eight. And I remember thinking — okay, I understand now. That's just what this life costs. And I think I just... I stopped looking for another way to cope, because why bother, right? You work, you drink, you die. That sounds darker than I mean it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No. It doesn't sound dark. It sounds honest. And it sounds like losing him took something from you that you haven't quite found a replacement for. I want to stay here for a second, if that's okay... You mentioned your partner. What do they see that worries them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She says I'm... not there. Even when I'm there, I'm not there. That by the time she wants to talk, I'm already — she says I go somewhere else. And I know what she means but I also... I don't know how to tell her that the alternative is worse. That without the drink, what she gets is this wound-up, snapping, miserable version of me that nobody wants around. The scotch makes me bearable.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're protecting her from a version of yourself you're afraid of. And somewhere in there, you're also protecting yourself from... something. What is it you think you'd have to feel, if the drink wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. That's not — I don't really do that. The introspective thing. I solve problems. External problems. I'm not very good at the... interior stuff. My therapist — I had a therapist, years ago — she used to say I had the emotional vocabulary of a golden retriever. Which, honestly, fair. ... I think I'd feel scared. If I'm being honest. I think it would just be fear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took courage to say. Real courage — more than most people bring into this room. Fear is... it makes so much sense given everything you've described. The pressure, your father, the sense that stopping means facing something enormous. You've been managing that fear for a long time. And I wonder — is it working? Is the managing working?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... No. I mean — the company's working. That part works. But the other stuff... she almost left last year. Did I mention that? She almost left. And I told her things would change and then they didn't, and she's still there, but it's like living with someone who's already half out the door. And I can close a deal with anyone on the planet but I cannot — I genuinely cannot figure out how to fix my own marriage.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've closed deals with everyone except the one person you most want to stay. ... Here's what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I'm getting it wrong: You've built something extraordinary, and you've paid for it with pieces of yourself you're not sure you can get back. The drink started as a tool and became a wall. And part of you — maybe a growing part — is wondering if there's a different way through. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that... that lands. I hate that it lands, but it does. I'm not — I'm not ready to say I have a problem, exactly. But I think I might be ready to say that what I've been doing isn't... it's not enough. It's not working well enough. And that's — coming from me, that is a significant statement.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is. And I want you to hear that — what you just did, right there, is hard. Genuinely hard. A man who's been running at full speed for fifteen years, sitting with this much uncertainty, and still choosing to look at it honestly... that matters. So I'm not going to push you anywhere today. But I am going to ask: what would it mean to you — for your marriage, for yourself — if things were even a little different six months from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think it would mean I actually showed up. Not just to work. Like, actually showed up. My wife deserves someone who's present. My kids are teenagers, they're almost gone, and I keep thinking I'll be present when things slow down and things never slow down. So I guess — yeah. Six months from now I'd want to be someone who's actually in the room. Not just occupying it.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab any seat, doesn't matter. I'm Jamie. I know walk-ins can feel a little weird, like you showed up to a party and you're not sure whose house it is. So — no agenda, no pressure. We can just talk. What brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... okay. Hi. I'm Mia. I'm, uh — honestly I'm not totally sure why I'm here. My HR person kind of pushed me to come after some stuff happened at work. I don't really know what this is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for showing up even when it wasn't totally your idea, Mia — that actually takes something. So what happened at work, if you're okay going there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I fell asleep in a meeting. Like, not just... nodded off. I full-on passed out and my manager had to wake me up. In front of like eight people. It was — god, it was mortifying. I've just been so exhausted. I have a four-month-old at home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four months. So you're right in the thick of it — and still dragging yourself to work on top of that. What's nights been like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Lily doesn't sleep more than two, maybe three hours at a stretch. So I'm up constantly. And I just... I started having a glass of wine to wind down, you know? To get out of my head for a bit. Except it's... it's not really one glass anymore. It kind of got away from me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say it got away from you — how much are we talking most nights?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: A bottle. Sometimes... more. I don't know, once I start I can't really stop. And I know how that sounds. I know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not here to impress me. What I'm hearing is someone who is completely depleted and found something that gives her twenty minutes of not feeling that way. That makes a lot of sense, even if it's starting to cost you things. You said you can't stop once you start — what's that like, being in that place?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... scary, kind of. Like I used to be someone who could have one glass and be done. And now one glass doesn't even — it doesn't touch it. And I tell myself every morning that tonight will be different. And then it's not. Every single night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds exhausting in a whole different way — like you're fighting yourself every day and losing. ... When you try to picture your life six months from now, what do you see?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I try not to picture it because... I don't know. More of the same, honestly. I can't really imagine feeling different than I do right now. That probably sounds terrible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound terrible. It sounds like someone who's lost hope a little bit. That's really different from being a bad person. ... You mentioned Lily. Tell me about her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's... she's amazing. She's only four months and she already has this whole personality. She makes these little sounds when I pick her up, like she — like she knows it's me. And I just... I don't want her to grow up seeing me like this. I don't want to be the mom who's always... foggy. I grew up with that and I swore I wouldn't be that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She already knows it's you. That means something. And what you just said — not wanting to be foggy for her, knowing what it felt like on the other side of that — what would it actually mean to you to be fully there for Lily?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. It would mean everything. Like... I had a mom who was checked out and I spent my whole childhood trying to get her attention. And here I am and Lily's not even a year old and I'm already... god. I hate that I'm doing this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I'm hearing because I don't want to miss it. You came in today because HR pushed you — but you still came. Underneath all the exhaustion, there's this really clear part of you that does not want to repeat what you experienced with your own mom. You can see that the drinking has gone past where you wanted it to go. And even though everything feels hopeless right now, when you talk about Lily, something in you lights up. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... I didn't think I'd be saying any of this out loud today but that's — that's right. That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage, Mia. And the fact that you can see all of this so clearly — that's not weakness, that's actually a strength. So — not a plan, not a commitment, just a question — what's one small thing that might make tonight feel even a little bit different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... texting my partner before I open the bottle. He's been worried and I keep telling him I'm fine and I'm clearly not fine. Maybe I could just — let him in a little. He'd want to help. I know he would.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really nice to meet you. I'm glad you came in today — it takes a lot to walk through that door, especially right after finishing a detox program. So... take your time. What's bringing you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... yeah. Hi. I, uh — I just finished the program last week, and they said I should see someone, and I found your information online so... I'm here, I guess. I don't really know where to start, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found your way here. That matters. It sounds like part of you is still figuring out what all of this means.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... logically I know I needed to stop. But I've had anxiety my whole life, and alcohol was just — it was the thing that made everything manageable. Parties, work events, even just like... going to dinner with people I don't know that well. Without it I kind of just... freeze up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's been doing something really important for you — helping you get through situations that feel almost impossible otherwise.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I — I used to think everyone felt that way, like oh I just need a drink to loosen up, totally normal. But then I started noticing I was calculating how many I could have before events. Making sure there was always alcohol wherever I was going. That's when I kind of... realized it was different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment of noticing — when the pattern became visible to you — that sounds like it was significant.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was. I mean, I still told myself it was fine for a while after that. But... yeah. Some part of me knew.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine going to one of those social situations now — without alcohol — what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Terror. Like, my heart starts racing just thinking about it right now. What if I don't know what to say? What if there's an awkward silence and everyone's just... looking at me? I know that sounds dramatic but it feels completely real when it's happening.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound dramatic at all. You've been carrying this anxiety for a long time, and alcohol has been the thing that made social life feel survivable. Of course imagining that without it feels terrifying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And that's — like, everyone always says just be yourself, and I'm like, okay, but my "self" can't make eye contact without wanting to disappear. The person I am at a party with a drink in my hand, that actually feels more like the real me than the one hiding in the corner. Does that make sense or does that sound completely insane?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense. And I'm curious — what would it mean to you if that version of you, the one who can be present and connect with people, could show up without needing alcohol to get her there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I've never really thought about it that way. I mean... that would be huge, actually. I've always wanted to just be comfortable around people without needing something to make me okay first. My friends — they don't even know how bad the anxiety really is. I've never had to let them see it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been protecting that part of yourself for a long time. And you're sitting here today, which tells me something — that some part of you is ready to find out if there's another way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think so. I mean, I'm still terrified. But... I also don't want to keep doing this. The detox was awful and I never — I never want to go through that again. And I'm just... I'm really tired. Tired of needing it every time I have to be around people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What might support look like for you as you start figuring out other ways to manage the anxiety? Are there things — even small ones — that have helped at all in the past?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've done therapy before, specifically for the anxiety — CBT, I think. It helped a little? And this is embarrassing but I downloaded a meditation app like three years ago and never touched it. I know exercise is supposed to help too but I never stick with it. I have ideas, I just... haven't actually done any of them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you. You came in today saying you didn't know where to start. And in this conversation you've been really clear — about what scares you, about what you want, about what you've already tried. You know CBT has helped. You have ideas waiting for you. And you just got through one of the hardest things a person can go through. That is not a small thing. You've thought about this more than you're giving yourself credit for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I guess I have been thinking about it. A lot, actually. I still feel really scared. But maybe... maybe it's actually possible? To be okay without it someday? I've never really let myself believe that before.
